READING GUIDE

How to use this edition




Each lecture, workshop and exercise is grouped under its source document. Pages extracted from
source PDFs are identified as Source page X/Y. Many slide decks use two-column layouts; text
from those columns is now read separately rather than mixed together.

Some equations use visual fraction bars, matrices, charts or tables that cannot be reliably repres‐
ented by plain text. The illustrated reader includes cropped visual references; this smaller text
edition omits those images to simplify uploading to AI tools. If a numerical result or equation
matters for an ----, verify it against the original source page.

Code is shown in monospaced blocks; long lines are visually wrapped to fit the page. Previews of
datasets and spreadsheets are not substitutes for complete working files.

This edition omits the requested institution/programme identifiers and associated contact links.
Check permissions before hosting or uploading teaching materials to third-party services.


  Hidden technical worksheets used by spreadsheet add-ins are omitted from this reading edition. The
  original Excel files remain unchanged.

  Introduction to R and RStudio

   Dr. Helen Wang

  R is a free, open-source programming language designed for statistical computing, data ana‐
    lysis, and graphical visualization. It is widely used in academia, research, and industry for
   tasks such as data cleaning, modeling, and visual storytelling.

   RStudio, on the other hand, is an integrated development environment (IDE) that provides a
   user-friendly interface for working with R. RStudio allows you to write code, save it for later
   use, display graphics, view results of your algorithms in a single convenient display.

   In short, R is the programming language itself, and RStudio is the software you use to interact
   with R.

   This guide will walk you through how to install R and RStudio on your computer. Both are free
   and open source, and for most people they should be straightforward to install. Please

     I.

   Installing R

  Go to the CRAN (Collective R Archive Network)– this is the site where R itself and most R
   packages live. Click on “Download R for XXX”, where XXX is either macOS or Windows:

   Figure 1: R Download Homepage

   [For Windows Users]

   After clicking on the third link of the webpage in Figure 1, you will be taken to the download
   page for Windows homepage (Figure 2). Click on “install R for the first time” and you will be





    SOURCE PAGE 2 / 9

   directed to the webpage as shown in Figure 3. Click on “Download R-4.6.1 for Windows” or the
   latest version displayed at the top of the page. Click Next through all the prompts to install like
   any other program. once finished, proceed to install R Studio.

   Note: Note: new releases of R are made regularly, therefore please ensure that you install the
   latest available (stable release) version, as indicated on the CRAN homepage.

   Figure 2: Download R for Windows, Webpage 1

   Figure 3: Download R for Windows, Webpage 2

    First upgrade to the latest macOS version and have Xcode Command Line Tools installed on

  C/C++ or Fortran code. To install the tool, run the following code in Terminal:

   xcode

   select

     If you run into problems with this code, go ahead and download the Xcode App from Apple
   Store.

   Then, click on the 2nd link on webpage of Figure 1 and you should be taken to the download
   page for macOS homepage, which looks like Figure 4.

   Pay attention to whether you need the ARM or the x86 version. If you are on the latest Mac
   M1, M2 chip click on “R-4.6.1-arm64.pkg” to download the ARM version, if you have an

   Figure 4: Download R for Mac

     II.

   RStudio

          a. Installing RStudio

   Please go to RStudio's homepage. (NOTE: You must have installed R before proceeding with
   the installation of RStudio). Scroll down to the bottom of the page where links for downloading
   RStudio for different operating systems are displayed as shown in Figure 5.





    SOURCE PAGE 4 / 9

   Click Next through all the prompts to install.

   Figure 5: RStudio Downloading Page

          b. Layout of RStudio

  Once installed, double-click on the RStudio icon to open the program. Click on “File → New File
  → R Script” to start a new R code file, then you will see the interface with four panes as shown
   in Figure 6, which is the most common layout for working with RStudio.

    SOURCE PAGE 5 / 9

   Figure 6: Default RStudio Interface (Windows)

   Console Pane (Bottom Left): This is where you interact directly with R. You can type and run R
  commands here, and the output (results, errors, etc.) will be shown immediately. For example,
   try typing “5 + 3”.

   Script Pane (Top Left): This is where you write and edit scripts, i.e., files containing code.

   You can run code line-by-line or in chunks into the Console. Note: there are two types of files
   that we will be working with:

        • R Script (.R file) is to be used when you are writing code for yourself. It consists of code
       and simple textual comments. It is more of a "developer" style of coding.

        • R Markdown (.Rmd file) is typically used when you plan to share your work with me, a
         colleague at work or in a presentation. It contains all the code, the results of running
        chunks of code, output images etc. When the file is completed, you can knit it to a pdf or
       an html format which you can share e.g. upload to Canvas.

   Workspace Pane (Top Right):

        • The Environment tab shows all active variables, data frames, and functions currently in
       memory.

        • The History tab lists all previously run commands, which you can reuse.





    SOURCE PAGE 6 / 9

   Display Pane (Bottom Right):

   graphics generated during session using Rcharts, htmlwidgets). Cannot be used for viewing
   online information.

        • The Files tab allows you to browse and manage files in your working directory.

        • The Plots tab allows you to view charts and graphs generated by your code.

        • In the Packages tab you can see installed packages and load/unload them.

        • In Help tab you can access documentation for R functions and packages.

        • The Viewer tab renders local web content in the form of static HTML pages (e.g. web

     III.

   Packages

  R packages are collections of functions, data, and documentation that extend the capabilities
   of base R. They allow you to perform specialized tasks without writing code from scratch.





SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                    7

PAGE 8
COURSE ----- READER                                                                       Pre-course Assignments


   The tidyverse is a collection of R packages designed for data analytics. These packages share
   a common philosophy, consistent grammar, and are built to work together. The tidyverse
   helps you with tasks like data cleaning, transformation, visualization, and modeling. For ex‐
   ample, ggplot2 is a package in the tidyverse which we will rely on for data visualization in this
   course.

   Please complete the courses “Introduction to the Tidyverse” and “Introduction to Data
   Visualisation with ggplot2” on Datacamp.

          a. Installing tidyverse

   You need to install all the packages you need before you can use them. As an example, I will
  show you the steps of installing tidyverse.

   To install tidyverse, go to the Display Pane and click on the Packages tab. Click on the “Install”
   button, and you will be directed to the window as displayed in Figure 8. Enter “tidyverse” (or
   any other package names later when you need them) in the “Packages” field, make sure to
   check the “Install dependencies” box, and click on “Install”.





    SOURCE PAGE 7 / 9

   Figure 7: The Packages Tab of Display Pane

   Figure 8: Installing tidyverse

          b. Loding tidyverse

  Once a package is installed on your machine it is saved in a directory called library. In order to
   use a package within RStudio it first needs to be loaded from the library using a command.
   Enter the following code in your Script Pane and run it by clicking on the green arrow-like “run”
   button on the top right side of the pane:


      library("tidyverse")





    SOURCE PAGE 8 / 9

   You will see outputs in the Console Pane telling you what packages have been loaded, as
  shown in Figure 9.

   Figure 9: Loding tidyverse

    IV. Posit AI Assistant

   From the 2026 version, RStudio has enabled an AI coding assistant function. It works more like
   an AI agent inside RStudio: it can see your R session, variables, console output, plots, and
   code, so you can ask it to write/debug R code, explain errors, explore a dataset, create
   visualisations, or help build models.

  Descriptive vs Inferential Statistics

   Descriptive Statistics

        • Collect

        • Organize

        • Summarize

        • Display

        • Analyze

   Typical Questions:

        • What is the average return per year of a stock?

        • Are stock returns Normally

   distributed?

   Inferential Statistics

        • Predict and forecast values of population parameters

        • ---- hypothesis and draw conclusions about values of population parameters

    SOURCE PAGE 14 / 63

  Why ----- Data Analytics?

   Data empowers decision-making in uncertain situations – financial analysts who harness the
   power of data in the face of uncertainty make better decisions.

   outcomei= modeli+ errori

    yi

    xi Systematic

    ei Unsystematic

   Part

   Part

   Statistics helps understand variability and make an inference – decisions should be grounded
   in statistical evidence. “Can trading signal extracted from a dataset be attributed to chance or
    is there a pattern?”

   Model: explains how much of the overall variance in the data can be explained by the model
   vs. the noise i.e., systematic (model variance) vs. unsystematic (random variance).

  Basic Data Types in R

   Every programming language comes with fundamental, pre-built objects that the programmer
   manipulates on a day-to-day basis.

   Atomic Class Example Definition

   Character "abc" 'abc' Data type used to store sequences of characters (we call it a ‘string’)

   Double 2.321

    Inf NaN

   Real number (double precision) In R, all numbers are converted to double by default. So, 3 in R
    is treated as 3.0 Inf – infinity (i.e., result of 1/0) NaN – not a number (i.e., result of 0/0); can
   also be thought of as a missing value

   Numeric

   Integer 3L as.integer(3)

   To create an integer, use L suffix (stands for Long integer, single precision)

   Logical TRUE FALSE NA

   Boolean logic, a variable denoting truth value: TRUE FALSE 1 is treated as TRUE, 0 is treated
   as FALSE NA – not available; is a filler for missing values

   In R (and most other coding languages), dimensionality is the number of indices needed to
   locate a data point.

  Data Dimensionality in Stats

   Indpendent variables data is usually structured as rows (observations) and columns (features /
   variables), overall called a Feature Matrix.

  A feature matrix X∈ℝN×D means there are N observations and D features, with elements xi,j
   referenced by i for rows and j for columns:

  D columns, j changes x1,1 x1,2 x1,3 … x2,1 x2,2 x2,3 … x3,1 x3,2 x3,3 … ⋮ ⋮ ⋮

  N rows, i changes

   Example: assume a feature matrix X∈ℝ1000×3, with 3 features (columns) x1, x2, x3.

  3 columns

   x1,1 x1,2 x1,3 x2,1 x2,2 x2,3 ⋮ x1000,1

  1000

  ⋮ x1000,2

  ⋮ x1000,3

   rows

  A single observation forms a row of the data.

   So, the first observation is a data point x1 = x1,1, x1,2, x1,3

   dimensionality of any data point in feature matrix X, such as x1, is D= 3.

    SOURCE PAGE 27 / 63

  Pipe Operator %>%

  3 equivalent ways to code the same thing:

  Why use the pipe operator?


      z <- 15.99 %>% round() %>% sqrt() %>% print()


        • Enhanced Workflow: the pipe connects multiple dplyr functions (‘verb’ / actions)
        together into a sequence of operations (‘pipeline’)

        • Consistency Across the Tidyverse: consistent syntax


      x <- round(15.99) y <- sqrt(x) z <- print(y)


   across dplyr, tidyr and ggplot2 libraries

        • Readability: the pipe takes output of one function and feeds it as input to the next
         function, making it easier to understand code


      z <- print(sqrt(round(15.99)))

    SOURCE PAGE 28 / 63

  Cleaning Data

   Stages of cleaning data:

        • Clean Column Headers: convert all names to lower case letters and separate spaces
         with an underscore

        • Convert Date from String to Date Format:

   timeseries data should be in a ‘Date’ format

        • Convert Categorical Variables to Factor / Numeric Format: instead of using strings for
         categorical variables it is best to store them as numbers in R’s memory

        • Remove Duplicate Rows: drop

   duplicates

        • Fill in Missing Data: either delete rows if they are missing any data, or forward fill the
        data from the last available data until the next

    SOURCE PAGE 39 / 63

  Untidy vs. Tidy Data

   Main ways in which data can be untidy:

          1. Column headers are values and not variable names

          2. A single observation unit is stored in multiple tables

          3. Multiple values are stored in one column



SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                   25

PAGE 26
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 1


          4. Variables are stored in both rows and columns

          5. Multiple types of observational units are stored in

   one table

   Data is tidy when:

          1. Data set is in ONE table

          2. Each column is a variable

          3. Each observation has its own row

          4. Each value has its own cell

   For programming examples see “R For Data Science” book, Chapter 12 ‘Tidy Data’.

  Verb: Select


      select() pick columns (variables) directly by the names


   Key Features:

        • No need for `` (use adj_close not "adj_close")

        Close use `Adj Close`)

   Example, select two columns:

   Example, select all columns between given columns:


      dji_ex2 <- dji_index %>% select(open:low)


   Example, select all but one columns:


      dji_ex3 <- dji_index %>% select(-ret)

  Verb: Arrange

  Verb: Mutate


      mutate() compute transformations on columns: create new columns using existing columns.


   Key Features:

        • Automatically adds new column to existing tibble

        • To drop all non-transformed variables use


      transmute()


   Example, perform feature engineering i.e. create a new feature (variable) using information
   from an existing feature. For example, create a 50-day moving average:


      dji_ex13 <- dji_index %>% mutate(ma50 = rollmean(adj_close, k = 50, fill = NA, align =
      "right"))


        • fill = NA fills the first 49 rows with missing values

        • align = "right" aligns rolling mean with the last day of the window (i.e. records the MA
          result into last day of the window)

  Verb: Group By


      group_by() group data into categories within a given variable.


   Key Features:

        • Does not change how data looks

        • Grouping changes how data acts with other verbs

        • Application of verbs on the resulting object will

   be performed by group

   Example, group by ’a’ and find mean of ‘b’:


      ex15 <- data %>% group_by(a) %>% summarise(mu_b = mean(b))


   Example, find mean return of DJI per year:


      ex16 <- dji_index %>% mutate(year = year(date)) %>% group_by(year) %>% summarise(mu_r =
      mean(ret))

    SOURCE PAGE 53 / 63

  Verb: Join


      xxx_join() join tibbles based on matching columns.


   tb1 tb2

   tb1 tb2 tb1 tb2

   tb1 tb2

    full join

   inner join

    left join

   right join

   Key Features:

        • First 2 arguments are tibbles to be joined

        • Results is always a new tibble

        • Argument by specifies which column should be used to match the observations in 2
         tables

    Full join keeps all data from both tables (i.e. all rows)


      dji_joined_full <- full_join(dji_table1, dji_table2, by = 'date')


   Inner join keeps only data for those dates that match (i.e. only matching rows).

   Left join keeps all rows from table 1 and only matching rows from table 2.

   Right join keeps all rows from table 2 and only matching rows from table 2.

  Data Visualization with ggplot2

   ggplot2 produces statistical graphs using grammar of graphics: components that can be put
   together.

    All plots are composed of:

        • Data – data stored in a tibble in a tidy format

        • Aesthetic mapping – specify x and y variables

        • Layers – made of ▪geoms (geometric objects) – represent objects visible on the plot
         (points / lines) ▪stats (statistical transformations) – summarise data by creating a linear
        model, histogram binning etc



SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                   34

PAGE 35
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 1


        • Faceting – break data into subsets

        • Theme – font size, background colour

        • Scales – colour, size, shape, legend, axes

   Typical Commands

        • aes() map a variable to x, map a variable to y

        • labs() label axes and title

        • geom_point() data as dots

        • geom_line() data as line

        • geom_historgram() data as histogram

        • geom_density() data as density

  Why ----- Data Analytics?

   Data empowers decision-making in uncertain situations – financial analysts who harness the
   power of data in the face of uncertainty make better decisions.

   outcomei= modeli+ errori

    yi

    xi Systematic

    ei Unsystematic

   Part

   Part

   Statistics helps understand variability and make an inference – decisions should be grounded
   in statistical evidence. “Can trading signal extracted from a dataset be attributed to chance or
    is there a pattern?”

   Model: explains how much of the overall variance in the data can be explained by the model
   vs. the noise i.e., systematic (model variance) vs. unsystematic (random variance).

  Basic Data Types in R

   Every programming language comes with fundamental, pre-built objects that the programmer
   manipulates on a day-to-day basis.

   Atomic Class Example Definition

   Character "abc" 'abc' Data type used to store sequences of characters (we call it a ‘string’)

   Double 2.321

    Inf NaN

   Real number (double precision) In R, all numbers are converted to double by default. So, 3 in R
    is treated as 3.0 Inf – infinity (i.e., result of 1/0) NaN – not a number (i.e., result of 0/0); can
   also be thought of as a missing value

   Numeric

   Integer 3L as.integer(3)

   To create an integer, use L suffix (stands for Long integer, single precision)

   Logical TRUE FALSE NA

   Boolean logic, a variable denoting truth value: TRUE FALSE 1 is treated as TRUE, 0 is treated
   as FALSE NA – not available; is a filler for missing values

  Data Dimensionality in Stats

   Indpendent variables data is usually structured as rows (observations) and columns (features /
   variables), overall called a Feature Matrix.

  A feature matrix X∈ℝN×D means there are N observations and D features, with elements xi,j
   referenced by i for rows and j for columns:

  D columns, j changes x1,1 x1,2 x1,3 … x2,1 x2,2 x2,3 … x3,1 x3,2 x3,3 … ⋮ ⋮ ⋮

  N rows, i changes

   Example: assume a feature matrix X∈ℝ1000×3, with 3 features (columns) x1, x2, x3.

  3 columns

   x1,1 x1,2 x1,3 x2,1 x2,2 x2,3 ⋮ x1000,1

  1000

  ⋮ x1000,2

  ⋮ x1000,3

   rows

  A single observation forms a row of the data.

   So, the first observation is a data point x1 = x1,1, x1,2, x1,3

COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 1


   T that resides in a multidimensional space.

   dimensionality of any data point in feature matrix X, such as x1, is D= 3.

  Pipe Operator %>%

  3 equivalent ways to code the same thing:

  Why use the pipe operator?


      z <- 15.99 %>% round() %>% sqrt() %>% print()


        • Enhanced Workflow: the pipe connects multiple dplyr functions (‘verb’ / actions)
        together into a sequence of operations (‘pipeline’)

        • Consistency Across the Tidyverse: consistent syntax


      x <- round(15.99) y <- sqrt(x) z <- print(y)


   across dplyr, tidyr and ggplot2 libraries

        • Readability: the pipe takes output of one function and feeds it as input to the next
         function, making it easier to understand code


      z <- print(sqrt(round(15.99)))

  Cleaning Data

   Stages of cleaning data:

        • Clean Column Headers: convert all names to lower case letters and separate spaces
         with an underscore

        • Convert Date from String to Date Format:

   timeseries data should be in a ‘Date’ format

        • Convert Categorical Variables to Factor / Numeric Format: instead of using strings for
         categorical variables it is best to store them as numbers in R’s memory

        • Remove Duplicate Rows: drop

   duplicates

        • Fill in Missing Data: either delete rows if they are missing any data, or forward fill the
        data from the last available data until the next

    SOURCE PAGE 40 / 65

  Untidy vs. Tidy Data

   Main ways in which data can be untidy:

          1. Column headers are values and not variable names

          2. A single observation unit is stored in multiple tables

          3. Multiple values are stored in one column

          4. Variables are stored in both rows and columns

          5. Multiple types of observational units are stored in

   one table

   Data is tidy when:

          1. Data set is in ONE table

          2. Each column is a variable

          3. Each observation has its own row

          4. Each value has its own cell

   For programming examples see “R For Data Science” book, Chapter 12 ‘Tidy Data’.

   DPLYR Package:

          1. Provides grammar manipulation which is a consistent set of verbs used to solve
      common data manipulation tasks

          2. Verbs are highly optimised through execution in C++ making them fast

          3. Used for problems with extracting rows and columns of interest as well as re-ordering
       and collapsing tibbles

   Key Features:

          1. Requirement: data typically should be in a

   tidy format

          2. Data Storage: data input and data output to and from dplyr functions is always a
          tibble

          3. Operator: %>% pipe

          4. Key Verbs: select, filter, arrange, rename, mutate, summarise, group_by

  Data Visualization with ggplot2

   ggplot2 produces statistical graphs using grammar of graphics: components that can be put
   together.

    All plots are composed of:

        • Data – data stored in a tibble in a tidy format

        • Aesthetic mapping – specify x and y variables

        • Layers – made of ▪geoms (geometric objects) – represent objects visible on the plot
         (points / lines) ▪stats (statistical transformations) – summarise data by creating a linear
        model, histogram binning etc

        • Faceting – break data into subsets

        • Theme – font size, background colour

        • Scales – colour, size, shape, legend, axes

   Typical Commands

        • aes() map a variable to x, map a variable to y

        • labs() label axes and title

        • geom_point() data as dots

        • geom_line() data as line

        • geom_historgram() data as histogram

        • geom_density() data as density

Exploratory Data Analysis for Dow Jones 30

We will use Dow Jones Index data, as well as Dow Jones individual constituents data, from 2010 to
2024 to demonstrate the steps that you should take when preparing data for analysis i.e. when
performing Exploratory Data Analysis.

We are working with R Markdown file type, which allows us to combine text, code, and output in a
single document, making it a powerful tool for data analysis, reporting, and reproducible re‐
search. You can knit this file to an HTML or pdf formats in order to share it with colleagues / man‐
agement.

Let's first load the data. Place the data and the .Rmd file in the same folder. Point RStudio to the
location of your files (go to Tools -\> Global Options -\> General -\> Default Working Directory -\>
Navigate to your directory -\> Apply -\> OK)


   dji_index_original <- read_csv('dji_index.csv')

Understanding Data Structure

Let's examine three things: \* Data types down each column of the data \* Dimensionality of your
data\ \* Observe statistical data summary down each column

Data Types

We would like to know what kind of data is stored in each column. We see that we have data
types:

     • <chr> character (i.e. data read in as text)

     • <dbl> double (i.e. data read in as numbers)


   glimpse(dji_index_original)


Dimensionality of Data

"Dimensionality of Data" means "how many columns (how many features / variables) do we have
that can be used as inputs into our model for data analysis"? When we make predicts we will typ‐
ically make models where $x$ variables (independent variables) are used to make a prediction of
a $y$ variable:

$y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 * x_1 + ... + \beta_m * x_m + error$

When we talk about 'dimensionality' we typically mean 'how many independent variables do I
have for analysis'?

In the DJI data's case, we can think of our data in the following way:

     • Date column: we can think of it as an observation number given by each date.

     • Assume that the data prediction task involves predicting the Adjusted Close of the DJI
      (usually we would try to predict if the DJI return was positive or negative rather than work‐
      ing with Adj Close directly). Therefore this column will form the y-label (the variable we are
      trying to predict).\

     • Therefore we can use 'High, Open, Low, Volume and Day Of Week' as the independent
      variables which can be input into our model to make predictions. Therefore the
      dimensionality of our data is 5.

Data Summary

Let's first create returns for the DJI Adjusted Closing prices.


   # create simple returns
   dji_index <- dji_index_original %>%
     mutate(ret = ( `Adj Close` / lag(`Adj Close`) - 1 ) * 100) %>%
     filter(!is.na(ret))

   # keep columns: date, returns and day of the week and store into a new variable
   dji_returns <- dji_index %>%
     select(Date, ret, `Day Of Week`)


We can use the Mosaic library function favstats() to find the min, max, std dev of the return data
i.e. to observe the basic statistics of the return feature / variable. Note the syntax of the
favstats() function: here you have a single numerical variable, hence use \~ x.



SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                   61

PAGE 62
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 1



   # Single numerical variable, use ~ x
   favstats(~ret, data=dji_returns)


We can also 'facet' analysis of the returns by day of the week to see if can suspect any significant
difference in the returns obtained on different days.


   # Single numerical variable and single categorical variable syntax: x ~ y
   favstats(ret ~ `Day Of Week`, data=dji_returns)


We can see that the mean return on Tuesdays seems higher than on the other days. This could be
due to outliers or potentially a signal we could investigate.

Cleaning Data

Clean Column Headers

Convert column headers to a conventional format: all lower case letters, any spaces to be re‐
placed with an underscore. To do this quickly, we use a package called JANITOR (already loaded at
the top of the file).


   dji_index <- dji_index %>%
     clean_names()


Convert String to Date

Change the strings in the column 'date' into a timestamp Date format.


   dji_index <- dji_index %>%
     mutate(date = dmy(date)) # Lubridate package of the Tidyverse, uses a function dmy() which
   stands for Date Month Year format


Convert String to Numeric Format

Change `day_of_week` variable to a numeric format (since it is harder to work with strings). We
will do this in two steps.

Convert string to factor first, i.e. provide both character and numeric representation to the cat‐
egorical data. Factor is a special data type (like string, numeric etc) which is used with categorical
data, where categories are called 'levels'. Internally, factors are stored as integers, where each
unique category is assigned a unique integer value, however if you look at the data it will display
strings. Therefore it is a flexible data type.


   dji_index <- dji_index %>%
     mutate(day_of_week = factor(day_of_week,
     levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"),
     ordered = TRUE))


Now obtain just the integer values of the factor and drop the string content, thereby converting
factor to numeric format.





SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                   62

PAGE 63
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 1



   dji_index <- dji_index %>%
     mutate(day_of_week = as.numeric(day_of_week))


When cleaning data we may encounter situations where the data we read in has missing values
or may have duplicate values. Let's assume we read in the data in such a format using a dataset
with missing values and duplicates, called 'dji_index_missing_and_duplicates.csv'.


   dji_index_unclean <- read_csv('dji_index_missing_and_duplicates.csv')


Remove Duplicates

Sometimes data may erroneously contain duplicated rows, let's check how many duplicates we
have:


   num_duplicated_rows <- dji_index_unclean %>%
     filter(duplicated(.)) %>%  # Filter only duplicated rows
     summarise(n = n())  # Count the number of duplicated rows

   print(num_duplicated_rows)


Duplicated rows should be removed:


   dji_index_unclean <- dji_index_unclean %>%
     distinct()


Fill in Missing Values

Sometimes data may be missing in some columns, lets examine how many missing values we
have in each column.


   missing_values_per_column <- dji_index_unclean %>%
     summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) # summarize works down columns

   print(missing_values_per_column)


We need to make a decision whether to delete rows with missing values, or since this is a time
series of stock Index data, forward fill the missing values so that not to introduce a forward look‐
ing bias. This means use the last available data and fill in the missing values using this data until
the next available data.


   dji_index_unclean <- dji_index_unclean %>%
     fill(everything(), .direction = "down")


We note that we still have 1 missing value in the first row since there was nothing to forward fill it
with. We can now drop the data with missing rows (i.e. the first row):


   dji_index_unclean <- dji_index_unclean %>%
     filter(complete.cases(.))

Data Wrangling: Tidy Data

When preparing data for analysis and working with the Tidyverse packages, it is important to
place the data into a format compatible with the Tidyverse framework.

Tidyverse is a collection of packages such as READR package (to read in data using read_csv()),
TIDYR package (to tidy data into a standard format), DPLYR package (to calculate statistics and
manipulate data),\ GGPLOT2 package (to visualize data), LUBRIDATE package (to work the dates if
using time series data) and more.

The key unifying feature of Tidyverse is that all data inputs and outputs from any functions
operate with data stored in a Tibble data structure.

Convert Data from Untidy to Tidy Format

As part of the Tidyverse framework, the data needs to be in a particular format we call 'tidy'.

Let's examine ways in which data can be untidy and convert it to a tidy format.

Column headers are values and not variable names

Current Dow Jones Index data is in the 'wide' (untidy) format i.e. values of the variable 'measure‐
ment' (High, Low, Open, Close etc) is spread across the columns. Instead they all should be
grouped into a single column called 'measurement'. Let's tidy up the data into a format Tidyverse
expects using a function pivot_longer() of the TIDYR package.


   dji_index_tidy <- dji_index %>%
     pivot_longer(cols = open:ret,
     names_to = "measurement",
     values_to = "value")


A single observation unit is stored in multiple tables

If the DJI data was stored as two tables (where a single unit called 'date' is present in both
tables), and one table contained 'high, open, low, adj_close', while the other contained 'volume'
measurements, then this is not considered a tidy format as the data set is meant to be in a single
table.

Hence these tables should be combined into a single table and converted to a tidy format.

You can combine the two tables using a full_join(x,y) function, and then convert the single
resulting table to a tidy format using pivot_longer() function.


   dji_table1 <- read_csv('dji_index_1.csv')
   dji_table2 <- read_csv('dji_index_2.csv')

   dji_joined <- full_join(dji_table1, dji_table2, by = 'date')

   dji_joined_tidy <- dji_joined %>%
     pivot_longer(cols = open:volume,
     names_to = "measurement",
     values_to = "value")





SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                   64

PAGE 65
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 1


Multiple varaibles are stored in one column

If the DJI data was stored as ratios of High/Low and Open/Adj_Close, then this is not considered a
tidy format as each value is expected to have its own cell.


   dji_table3 <- read_csv('dji_index_3.csv')
   glimpse(dji_table3)


We need to separate the data and then pivot_longer() to convert the data into a tidy format. Let's
separate the ratios into single columns first.

Note: convert=TRUE is needed in order to let R automatically recognize the data type of the new
columns. Here they will be recognized as numeric data type. If you do not do this, they will be
kept as characters.


   dji_split <- dji_table3 %>%
     separate(`high/low`, into = c("high", "low"), convert=TRUE) %>%
     separate(`open/adj_close`, into = c("open", "adj_close"), convert=TRUE)

   glimpse(dji_split)


Now pivot the data to obtain the long format.


   dji_split_tidy <- dji_split %>%
     pivot_longer(cols = volume:adj_close,
     names_to = "measurement",
     values_to = "value")

   glimpse(dji_split_tidy)


For further programming examples of untidy data see “R For Data Science” book, Chapter 12
‘Tidy Data’.

Pivot Back From Long (Tidy) to Wide (Untidy) If Needed

In case you would like to convert back to a wide format for some reason, you can do so with the
pivot_wider() function, which spreads the data across columns.


   dji_index_untidy <- dji_index_tidy %>%
     pivot_wider(names_from = measurement,
     values_from = value)

   glimpse(dji_index_untidy)

Data Wrangling: Manipulating Data

The DPLYR library allows us to manipulate data in a variety of ways. This library expects data to
be in a tidy format (i.e. long format), however for certain verbs it is easier to work with the wide
format, for example:

DPLYR vs. R Base

DPLYR allows you to manipulate the data through a series of verbs connected with pipe operators,
which makes your code tidy and easy to read. The example below shows you how to compute the
mean of all positive returns through DPLYR vs. R base.

DPLYR:


   r_mu_pipe <- dji_index_original %>%
     mutate(ret = ( `Adj Close` / lag(`Adj Close`) - 1 ) * 100) %>%
     filter(!is.na(ret)) %>%
     filter(ret > 0) %>%
     summarise(r_mu = mean(ret))


R Base:


   r_mu_base <- data.frame(r_mu = mean(((dji_index_original$`Adj Close` / c(NA,
   head(dji_index_original$`Adj Close`, -1)) - 1) * 100)[((dji_index_original$`Adj Close` / c(NA,
   head(dji_index_original$`Adj Close`, -1)) - 1) * 100) > 0], na.rm = TRUE))

Verb Group By

Group By with Summarise

Grouping the data by year first, before finding the mean return, would allow us to obtain more
information i.e. to obtain mean return per year.

Let's create a new column called 'year' using Lubridate package first.


   dji_index <- dji_index %>%
     mutate(year = year(date),
     month = month(date)) # can also create month for example

   print(dji_index)


Let's observe if grouping this tibble by year creates any visual change to the data. Observe that
visually there is no change. We only see at the top that we have grouped the data by year and
that there are 15 groups (i.e. 15 years).


   dji_ex15 <- dji_index %>%
     group_by(year) # group by year so that subsequent operations are applied per group





SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                   69

PAGE 70
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 1




   print(dji_ex15)


Let's now find mean return of the DJI per each year.


   dji_ex16 <- dji_index %>%
     group_by(year) %>%
     summarise(mu_r = mean(ret))

   print(dji_ex16)


We can also count the number of observations within each group (in this case it will be the num‐
ber of days in each working year). There are typically 252 trading days in a year, but we can see
some small variation.


   dji_ex17 <- dji_index %>%
     group_by(year) %>%
     summarise(count = n())

   print(dji_ex17)


We can also use group_by with mutate and arrange verbs to allow us to examine information by
group.

Group By with Mutate

Let's see an example of grouping followed by mutate. Let's find the z-value of the returns per
year. Reminder the z-value is found using the formula:

$z_i = \frac{x_i - \bar{x}}{s}$, where $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean and $s$ is the sample
standard deviation.

Let's assume we would like to find the z-value of our data pear year, i.e. we will use the sample
mean and sample standard deviation per year to adjust our returns into z-values.


   dji_ex18 <- dji_index %>%
     group_by(year) %>%
     mutate(ret_z = (ret - mean(ret) / sd(ret)))


Q: if we don't use the grouping by year first, how will ret_r be different?

Group By with Arrange

We can re-order data based on a column of interest, for example year again. Let's order our re‐
turns data in *descending* order by year. Note: that in order to arrange using groups, we need to
specify .by_group = TRUE


   dji_ex19 <- dji_index %>%
     group_by(year) %>%
     arrange(desc(ret), .by_group = TRUE)


     Q. If we wanted to arrange returns by year in *ascending* order, what do we need to
     change in the code?

Verb Join

Full Join

Keep all data from both tables regardless if dates match, i.e. keep all dates data from table 1 and
all dates data from table 2. Remember we have already done this above, when we had to tidy a
dataset stored across 2 tables. In that case all the dates matched anyway.


   dji_joined <- full_join(dji_table1, dji_table2, by = 'date')


Let's say we have a Shanghai Stock Exchange Composite Index (sse.csv) that we would like to
combine with the S&P500 Index data. Both data sets contain data from 14/05/2010 to
15/05/2020. Sometimes these trade on different dates due to holidays, therefore the different
ways of joining data will be demonstrated better. Note that we have 2517 observations for
S&P500 and 2427 observations for SSE.

Read in both indices data:


   sse_index <- read_csv('sse_index.csv')
   snp_index <- read_csv('snp_index.csv')

   # convert first column to Date datatype (rather than string)
   sse_index <- sse_index %>%
     mutate(date = dmy(date))

   snp_index <- snp_index %>%
     mutate(date = dmy(date))


Inner Join

Only keep data for matching dates. We note that there are 2346 matching dates.


   indices_join_inner <- inner_join(sse_index, snp_index, by = 'date')


Left Join

Keep all of the dates for SSE, but only matching S&P. We note that all 2427 rows of SSE were
kept, but missing values of S&P are present on dates when it did not trade.


   indices_join_left <- left_join(sse_index, snp_index, by = 'date') %>%
     arrange(date)


Right Join

Keep all of the dates for S&P, but only matching SSE. We note that all 2517 rows of S&P were
kept, but missing values of SSE are present on dates when it did not trade.


   indices_join_right <- right_join(sse_index, snp_index, by = 'date') %>%
     arrange(date)

  Nomenclature

   Population mean: μ Sample mean: x̄

   Population standard deviation: σ Sample standard deviation: s

  Random variable: X Particular observation: x

  Random variable of a Standard Normal: Z Particular observation of a Standard Normal (also
  known as ‘z-critical value’): z

   Cumulative Density Function of Standard Normal: Φ z

   Probability random variable Z takes on a value less than or equal to z: PZ≤z

   Standard Error: SE

   Parameter of t-distribution (also known as ‘degrees of freedom’): υ t-critical value: t

  Probability Distributions

   Definition

   Probability Distribution:

   Let’s roll dice!

        • If an infinite number of observations was obtained, what would the frequency of data
       be like?

        • Expression that describes the relative frequency for every possible outcome or a range
         of outcomes.

        • Represents the real-world model “well enough” – even though nothing in the real world
           is exactly distributed as the suspected probability distribution.

   Describing Probability Distributions

        • Shape: symmetry, modality, skewness





SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                   94

PAGE 95
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 2


        • Central Tendency: estimate of a typical observation in the distribution (mean, median,
       mode)

        • Spread: measure of variability in a distribution (range, variance, standard deviation,
        IQR)

        • Unusual Observations: observations that standout from the rest of the data that may
       be suspected outliers

  Higher Moments


      Skewness (3rd Moment)


        • Measure of asymmetry : a perfectly symmetrical distribution has skewness of 0.

        • Positive Skew tail pointing to high values (body of the distribution is to the left)

        • Negative Skew tail pointing to low values (body of the distribution is to the right)


      Kurtosis (4th Moment)


        • Measure of heaviness of the tails: measures the peakedness of a distribution

        • Leptokurtic : sharper peak, heavier tails, more

    outliers.

        • Platykurtic : flatter top, light tails, fewer

    SOURCE PAGE 19 / 63

  Properties of Normal Distribution

   Key Features

          1. Symmetric: scores are concentrated in the middle.

   Skewness = 0, Kurtosis (excess) = 0

          2. Parameters: distribution can be described with the location (mean) and scale
         (variance) parameters.

          3. Empirical rule for Normal Distributions: how likely is it to find a datapoint within
         certain number of standard deviations from the mean?

   χ Three-Sigma Rule

  68% of the data lies within one standard deviation (±0.99σ) of the mean 95% of the data lies
   within two standard deviations (±1.96σ) of the mean 99.7% of the data lies within three
   standard deviations (±2.97σ) of the mean

COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 2

    SOURCE PAGE 21 / 63

  Example: Normality Assumption

   Pizza Delivery Times

   Assuming Normally Distributed delivery times, the owner of Val’s Pizza decided to run an ex‐
   periment. He found that sample mean delivery time was 30min and sample variance was
   25min.

   Q: Given this knowledge what range of delivery times can customers expect 68%, 95%, 99.7%
   of the time?

   A:

  68% of deliveries are 30min ± 1 ∗5min = 25-35 min 95% of deliveries are 30min ± 2 ∗5min
  = 20-40 min 99.7% of deliveries are 30min ± 3 ∗5min = 15-45 min

  Standard Normal Distribution

   z-score: number of standard deviations an observation falls above or below mean.

  Z= X−μ

   σ Key Features:

        • A special case of the Normal Distribution where µ = 0 and σ= 1 i.e. Z∼N(µ = 0, σ2 =
          1).

        • Creates a common scale so you can access and compare different data without
        depending on the specific unit it was measured in

        • If population parameters are not known, use sample statistics, i.e., x̄and s.




SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                   99

COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 2


        • There is a 99.7% chance of being within ±2.97σof the mean, i.e. most values are
        contained within [-3,+3]

  Cumulative Density Function

   Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of a Standard Normal distribution, Φ z , provides the
   probability, p, that a Standard Normally distributed random variable (r.v.) Z, that has µ = 0
   and σ= 1, is less than or equal to a particular value z

  Φ z= PZ< z= PZ≤z

   where PZ≤z equivalently:

    SOURCE PAGE 31 / 63

  Why Convert Normal to Standard Normal?

   Advantage of using z-values:

  Any Normal distribution can be converted to Standard Normal, i.e. x observations converted to
   z-scores in range of approx. [-3, 3]. This results in:

        • Values on a consistent scale irrespective of the original parameters

        • Ability to use a table to find the probabilities associated with events, P(Z< z)

        • Use of statistical methods that rely on properties of Standard Normal distribution, e.g.

   Confidence Intervals, Hypothesis -------, Regression Parameters Estimation

        • Easier understanding of how many σ a value is away from the mean, since z∗σ= z∗1
     = z

    SOURCE PAGE 33 / 63

   Inferential Statistics

   Descriptive Statistics:

        • Describe the whole population (everyone we are interested in) – typically difficult to
         obtain.

        • Properties calculated (mean, standard deviation) are called parameters (the TRUTH).

        • Population parameters refer to the perfect knowledge; we reserve Greek letters (μ, σ)
          for them.

   Inferential Statistics:

        • Use a (random) sample to infer unknown population

   parameters.





SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  103

PAGE 104
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 2


        • Properties calculated are called sample statistics, e.g.

   sample mean, x̄, sample standard deviation, s, which are used to estimate parameters of the
   population (i.e. make an inference).

        • Different samples will typically have different sample

    statistics.

        • Applications using sampling: Finance, Healthcare,

    Politics, Quality Control.

        • Why sample? Cost efficiency, -----to-distruction,

   Reduce risk to patients.





    SOURCE PAGE 34 / 63

   Statistics is a Science of Inference

    Statistical Inference:

        • Predict and forecast values of population parameters.

        • ---- hypothesis about values of population parameters.

        • Make decisions.

        • Challenge: do this based on sample statistics derived from limited and incomplete
        sample information.

  Make generalizations about the characteristics of a population...

  On the basis of observations of a sample, a part of a population.





    SOURCE PAGE 35 / 63

  Sampling Error

  We are interested in the true mean of a population, μ.

   Since populations are difficult to collect data on, we use sample statistics (sample mean, x̄) as
   point estimate for the unknown true population parameter.

   Sample statistics vary from sample to sample due to sampling error, an error arising from the
   unrepresentativeness of sample taken (from observing a sample instead of whole population).

   Quantifying sampling error (how sample statistics vary from sample to sample) provides a way
   to estimate the margin of error associated with our point estimate.

   Sampling Error Example:

  Assume population mean is unknown, and we want to get an estimate on it. Take a sample of
   size n = 5.



SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  104

PAGE 105
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 2


   Population: μ= 32.0, σ= 3.3

   x̄= 31.6 x̄= 33.0 x̄= 35.2

  We see variation in sample means.

        • represents the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean.

   SE = σ

  Central Limit Theorem

   Start with a random variable X that belongs to some (any) distribution with known mean μ and
   std dev σ.

   Obtain a large sample n of independent observations of a random variable X and find the
   sample mean x̄.

   Central Limit Theorem states that: the distribution of sample mean, തX, will approach a Nor‐
   mal distribution as sample size n increases (n≥30), with mean μ and standard deviation σ

   n, i.e.,

  തX ~ Nμ, σ2

   n.

   Note: standard deviation of the distribution of sample means is known as the Standard Error,

   σ

   n.

   Sampling distribution of the sample mean

  σ2

    r.v. തX ~Nμ,

   n

   Population distribution r.v. X ~ dist(μ, σ)

   Simulation: https://onlinestatbook.com/stat_sim/samp ling_dist/

  Motivation: Communicating Uncertainty

   Example, Apricot Company:

        • You have recently joined the marketing department of Apricot, a mobile phone
        competitor to iPhone.

        • Your task is to find out how much people are willing to pay (WTP) on average for your
        company’s new mobile phone, which is thinner and lighter than the iPhone.

        • You conduct a quick survey and ask n= 100 people for their WTP and find that the
        average amount is £200 (i.e. x̄= 200)

   Task:

    SOURCE PAGE 44 / 63

  Confidence Interval Approximation

  Why form Confidence Intervals?

   Problem: often we don’t know the population mean, μ.

   Solution: use sample mean and make an inference about the population mean.

   Inference:

        • We report an interval within which we are 95% confident that the true population
      mean resides.

        • Since distribution of sample means is Normal, and we want to be 95% certain, we use
         properties of the Normal dist. to establish the confidence interval.

  How to From Confidence Intervals?

   Sample means distribution is Normal തX ~ Nμ, σ2

   n,

   σ

    i.e. the distribution’s standard deviation is

   n which

    is also known as the Standard Error.

  We can form an interval around the sample mean using the information about the margin of
   error (i.e. the Standard Error), using the following equation:

     x̄ ± z∗Standard Error

  What is the rational for doing this? We want to capture 95% body of the Normal Distribution,
    i.e. be 95% certain.





    SOURCE PAGE 45 / 63

  Confidence Interval Approximation

   Confidence Interval (CI) is a range of values derived from a sample that is expected to contain
   the true population parameter μ.

        • CI is expressed with a level of confidence, that is typically expressed as a percentage,
          e.g. 95%.

        • Level of confidence means if we were to take many samples and construct a CI for
        each, approx. 95% of them would contain the true parameter.

   CI Formula:

   Point Estimate ± Margin of Error =



SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  109

PAGE 110
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 2


     x̄ ± z∗Standard Error where z-value depends on the level of confidence.

   Example: 95% Confidence Interval To build a CI around sample mean which leaves us 95%
   confident, we need to select the value of z such that in total 5% is left in the tails, i.e. z= 1.96

  95% 2.5% 2.5%

     x̄ – 1.96×SE x̄ x̄ + 1.96×SE





    SOURCE PAGE 46 / 63

  Establishing z-value for CI


      z <- qnorm(0.975, mean = 0, sd = 1)


   The Quantile function qnrom() returns the zvalue corresponding to the specified probability p
   from the equation P(Z< z) = p.

     If we would like 95% probability to be left in the body of the distribution, that means we need
  2.5% to be left in each tail.

   The qnorm() function returns z-value corresponding to the probability to the left of the z-value.
   Therefore p=0.975 is should be used.

  z= 1.96

   [1] 1.96

   Thus, we can form a 95% CI using: x̄ ± 1.96×SE

   You took a sample with n= 2 observations from a uniform distribution in range [10, 30] (mean
  μ= 20 and std dev σ= 5.7735, both unknown to you).

   Suppose observations are: x1 = 15.167 and x2 = 16.708, then the sample mean is x̄=
   15.9375 and sample std dev is s= 1.09

     If we apply the usual CI formula, we get: 15.9375

   1.09

  ± 1.96 ×

  2 = 15.9375 ± 1.5107 ≈[14.42, 17.45]

   The range is far from true mean 20, what happened?

   Solution:

  How do we account for the fact we do not know the population standard deviation and instead
   used the sample standard deviation but with access to only a small sample size?

  Make a larger confidence interval reflecting our uncertainty, i.e. instead of z= 1.96, we use
   another larger value.

   Let’s introduce the -------’s t-distribution.





    SOURCE PAGE 55 / 63

   -------’s t-Distribution

   t-distribution

        • Has thicker tails than Normal (i.e. larger chance of extreme events).

        • Its shape depends on a single parameter “nu” ν= n – 1, where n is the number of ob‐
         servations.

        • When n≥30 t-distribution is considered sufficiently close to Normal for practical
         application purposes.

        • Example: t11−1 is a t-distribution with ν= 10

   t-distribution vs Standard Normal


      N(0, 1)


   t4-1

  n=4 n=11 t11-1

   ν is also called “Degree of Freedom”.

    SOURCE PAGE 62 / 63

  Summary: Confidence Intervals

   Sample statistic ≠ population parameter.

   But if the sample is good, it can be a good estimate.

   Report an estimate with a confidence interval Width of the interval depends on how variable
   sample statistics would be from different samples and the confidence level used (e.g. typical
   level is 95%).

  95% Confidence Level If you take many samples and compute a CI around each sample mean,
   then 95% of those intervals would contain the true mean. It is not a statement about a single
   sample mean is the true mean, i.e. we are NOT saying that we are 95% certain that the
   population parameter is X.

  Nomenclature

   Population mean: μ Sample mean: x̄

   Population standard deviation: σ Sample standard deviation: s

  Random variable: X Particular observation: x

  known as ‘z-critical value’): z

   Cumulative Density Function of Standard Normal: Φ z

   Probability random variable Z takes on a value less than or equal to z: PZ≤z

   Standard Error: SE

   Parameter of t-distribution (also known as ‘degrees of freedom’): υ t-critical value: t

  Probability Distributions

   Definition

   Probability Distribution:

   Let’s roll dice!

        • If an infinite number of observations was obtained, what would the frequency of data
       be like?

        • Expression that describes the relative frequency for every possible outcome or a range
         of outcomes.

        • Represents the real-world model “well enough” – even though nothing in the real world
           is exactly distributed as the suspected probability distribution.

   Describing Probability Distributions

        • Shape: symmetry, modality, skewness





SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  120

PAGE 121
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 2


        • Central Tendency: estimate of a typical observation in the distribution (mean, median,
       mode)

        • Spread: measure of variability in a distribution (range, variance, standard deviation,
        IQR)

        • Unusual Observations: observations that standout from the rest of the data that may
       be suspected outliers

      Skewness (3rd Moment)


        • Measure of asymmetry : a perfectly symmetrical distribution has skewness of 0.

        • Positive Skew tail pointing to high values (body of the distribution is to the left)

        • Negative Skew tail pointing to low values (body of the distribution is to the right)

    outliers.

    SOURCE PAGE 19 / 74

  Properties of Normal Distribution

   Key Features

          1. Symmetric: scores are concentrated in the middle.

   Skewness = 0, Kurtosis (excess) = 0

          2. Parameters: distribution can be described with the location (mean) and scale
         (variance) parameters.

          3. Empirical rule for Normal Distributions: how likely is it to find a datapoint within
         certain number of standard deviations from the mean?

   χ Three-Sigma Rule

  68% of the data lies within one standard deviation (±0.99σ) of the mean 95% of the data lies
   within two standard deviations (±1.96σ) of the mean 99.7% of the data lies within three
   standard deviations (±2.97σ) of the mean

  Example: Normality Assumption

   Pizza Delivery Times

   Assuming Normally Distributed delivery times, the owner of Val’s Pizza decided to run an ex‐
   periment. He found that sample mean delivery time was 30min and sample variance was
   25min.

   Q: Given this knowledge what range of delivery times can customers expect 68%, 95%, 99.7%
   of the time?

   A:

  68% of deliveries are 30min ± 1 ∗5min = 25-35 min 95% of deliveries are 30min ± 2 ∗5min
  = 20-40 min 99.7% of deliveries are 30min ± 3 ∗5min = 15-45 min

  Standard Normal Distribution

   z-score: number of standard deviations an observation falls above or below mean.

  Z= X−μ

   σ Key Features:

        • A special case of the Normal Distribution where µ = 0 and σ= 1 i.e. Z∼N(µ = 0, σ2 =
          1).

        • Creates a common scale so you can access and compare different data without
        depending on the specific unit it was measured in

        • If population parameters are not known, use sample statistics, i.e., x̄and s.

   Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of a Standard Normal distribution, Φ z , provides the
   probability, p, that a Standard Normally distributed random variable (r.v.) Z, that has µ = 0
   and σ= 1, is less than or equal to a particular value z

  Φ z= PZ< z= PZ≤z

   where PZ≤z equivalently:

  Why Convert Normal to Standard Normal?

   Advantage of using z-values:

  Any Normal distribution can be converted to Standard Normal, i.e. x observations converted to
   z-scores in range of approx. [-3, 3]. This results in:

        • Values on a consistent scale irrespective of the original parameters

        • Ability to use a table to find the probabilities associated with events, P(Z< z)

        • Use of statistical methods that rely on properties of Standard Normal distribution, e.g.

   Confidence Intervals, Hypothesis -------, Regression Parameters Estimation

        • Easier understanding of how many σ a value is away from the mean, since z∗σ= z∗1
     = z

   Inferential Statistics

   Descriptive Statistics:

        • Describe the whole population (everyone we are interested in) – typically difficult to
         obtain.

        • Properties calculated (mean, standard deviation) are called parameters (the TRUTH).

        • Population parameters refer to the perfect knowledge; we reserve Greek letters (μ, σ)
          for them.

   Inferential Statistics:

        • Use a (random) sample to infer unknown population

   parameters.

        • Properties calculated are called sample statistics, e.g.

   sample mean, x̄, sample standard deviation, s, which are used to estimate parameters of the
   population (i.e. make an inference).

        • Different samples will typically have different sample

        sample information.

  Make generalizations about the characteristics of a population...

  Sampling Error

  We are interested in the true mean of a population, μ.

   Since populations are difficult to collect data on, we use sample statistics (sample mean, x̄) as
   point estimate for the unknown true population parameter.

   Sample statistics vary from sample to sample due to sampling error, an error arising from the
   unrepresentativeness of sample taken (from observing a sample instead of whole population).

   Quantifying sampling error (how sample statistics vary from sample to sample) provides a way
   to estimate the margin of error associated with our point estimate.

   Sampling Error Example:

  Assume population mean is unknown, and we want to get an estimate on it. Take a sample of
   size n = 5.

   Population: μ= 32.0, σ= 3.3

   x̄= 31.6 x̄= 33.0 x̄= 35.2

  We see variation in sample means.

  Confidence Interval Approximation

  Why form Confidence Intervals?

   Problem: often we don’t know the population mean, μ.

   Solution: use sample mean and make an inference about the population mean.

   Inference:

        • We report an interval within which we are 95% confident that the true population
      mean resides.

        • Since distribution of sample means is Normal, and we want to be 95% certain, we use
         properties of the Normal dist. to establish the confidence interval.

  How to From Confidence Intervals?

   Sample means distribution is Normal തX ~ Nμ, σ2

   n,

    i.e. the distribution’s standard deviation is σ

   n which

    is also known as the Standard Error.

  We can form an interval around the sample mean using the information about the margin of
   error (i.e. the Standard Error), using the following equation:

     x̄ ± z∗Standard Error

  What is the rational for doing this? We want to capture 95% body of the Normal Distribution,
    i.e. be 95% certain.





SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  138

COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 2



    SOURCE PAGE 53 / 74

  Confidence Interval Approximation

   Confidence Interval (CI) is a range of values derived from a sample that is expected to contain
   the true population parameter μ.

        • CI is expressed with a level of confidence, that is typically expressed as a percentage,
          e.g. 95%.

        • Level of confidence means if we were to take many samples and construct a CI for
        each, approx. 95% of them would contain the true parameter.

   CI Formula:

   Point Estimate ± Margin of Error =

     x̄ ± z∗Standard Error where z-value depends on the level of confidence.

   Example: 95% Confidence Interval To build a CI around sample mean which leaves us 95%
   confident, we need to select the value of z such that in total 5% is left in the tails, i.e. z= 1.96

  95% 2.5% 2.5%

     x̄ – 1.96×SE x̄ x̄ + 1.96×SE





    SOURCE PAGE 54 / 74

  Establishing z-value for CI


      z <- qnorm(0.975, mean = 0, sd = 1)


   The Quantile function qnrom() returns the zvalue corresponding to the specified probability p
   from the equation P(Z< z) = p.

     If we would like 95% probability to be left in the body of the distribution, that means we need
  2.5% to be left in each tail.

   The qnorm() function returns z-value corresponding to the probability to the left of the z-value.
   Therefore p=0.975 is should be used.

  z= 1.96

   [1] 1.96

   Thus, we can form a 95% CI using: x̄ ± 1.96×SE

  CI for Small Samples, n< 30

   Motivating Example:

   You took a sample with n= 2 observations from a uniform distribution in range [10, 30] (mean
  μ= 20 and std dev σ= 5.7735, both unknown to you).

   Suppose observations are: x1 = 15.167 and x2 = 16.708, then the sample mean is x̄=
   15.9375 and sample std dev is s= 1.09

     If we apply the usual CI formula, we get: 15.9375 ±

   1.09

   1.96 ×

  2 = 15.9375 ± 1.5107 ≈[14.42, 17.45]

   The range is far from true mean 20, what happened?

   Solution:

  How do we account for the fact we do not know the population standard deviation and instead
   used the sample standard deviation but with access to only a small sample size?

  Make a larger confidence interval reflecting our uncertainty, i.e. instead of z= 1.96, we use
   another larger value.

   Let’s introduce the -------’s t-distribution.

   -------’s t-Distribution

   t-distribution

        • Has thicker tails than Normal (i.e. larger chance of extreme events).

        • Its shape depends on a single parameter “nu” ν= n – 1, where n is the number of ob‐
         servations.

        • When n≥30 t-distribution is considered sufficiently close to Normal for practical
         application purposes.

        • Example: t11−1 is a t-distribution with ν= 10

   t-distribution vs Standard Normal


      N(0, 1)


   t4-1

  n=4 n=11 t11-1

   ν is also called “Degree of Freedom”.

    SOURCE PAGE 73 / 74

  Summary: Confidence Intervals

   Sample statistic ≠ population parameter.

   But if the sample is good, it can be a good estimate.

   Report an estimate with a confidence interval Width of the interval depends on how variable
   sample statistics would be from different samples and the confidence level used (e.g. typical
   level is 95%).

  95% Confidence Level If you take many samples and compute a CI around each sample mean,
   then 95% of those intervals would contain the true mean. It is not a statement about a single
   sample mean is the true mean, i.e. we are NOT saying that we are 95% certain that the
   population parameter is X.

Treasury securities and their time to maturity.

     '30-Year Treasury Rate')

   # By default R will sort these maturities alphabetically; but since we want to keep them in
   that exact order, we recast maturity as a factor with the levels defined in the order of the
   maturity variable elements
   maturity <- factor(maturity, levels = maturity)

   # create a look up container
   mylookup <- tibble(symbol = tickers,
     var = myvars,
     maturity = maturity)

   # examine as a table
   mylookup %>%
     kable("html", col.names = c("Symbol", "Description", "Maturity")) %>%

     full_width = FALSE) %>%
     column_spec(1, bold = TRUE) %>%
     row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, background = "#D3D3D3") %>%
     add_header_above(c("Treasury Data" = 3))

Combine the downloaded data with our lookup table.

Note that here we use the left_join() verb because we judge that the treasury_data contains the
most important information (data), all of which should be kept. While the lookup table is simply a
reference table of names hence only the matching names should be attached into treasury_data.


   yield_curve <- left_join(treasury_data, mylookup, by = "symbol") %>%
     rename(value = price) %>%
     mutate(duration = factor(var, levels = myvars)) # also create a duration as a factor rather
   than string (var)

Feature Engineering for a Trading Signal

As part of building a trading model, we may include variables which indicate to the model wheth‐
er an 'extreme / unexpected' value is being observed. As such let's calculate a dummy variable
which will indicate to us if the contract's value is more/less than 2 standard deviations away from
the mean.

To do this calculation, we first need to use group_by() the data by symbol (which corresponds ma‐
turity). Next we calculate the returns for each maturity, and then convert to our data to z-scores.

Remember since we group_by() first, the subsequent verb operations are performed on the group
rather than on the whole column.

Note that our data is in the tidy long format ready for dplyr verb application.


   yield_curve_z <- yield_curve %>%
     group_by(symbol) %>%
     mutate(ret = (value / lag(value) - 1) * 100) %>%
     filter(!is.na(ret)) %>%
     mutate(ret_z = (ret - mean(ret)) / sd(ret)) %>%
     ungroup()


Q: Why are we working with returns rather than prices?

Let's plot the distribution of returns vs the distribution of the z-scores for 2 year maturity.


   # First plot for the returns distribution (`ret`)
   yield_curve_z %>%
     filter(symbol %in% c('GS2')) %>%

     ggplot(aes(x = ret, fill = symbol)) +
     geom_density(alpha = 0.4, colour = "red") +

     theme(
     plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
     axis.title = element_text(size = 14),

We can see that the distributions look similar to Normal but with more probability in the tails than
the Standard Normal. How do I know that? (What values does the Standard Normal typically cut
off at?)

[EXTRA]: We can perform an official statistical significance ---- to see if a given dataset is Nor‐
mally distributed. This is called the Shapiro-Wilk ----. We assume by default (H0, null hypothesis),
that the data is Normally distributed. The alternative belief then is that it is not Normal (H1, al‐
ternative hypothesis). We uphold the null hypothesis unless we can reject it beyond reasonable
doubt (which is if the p-value < 0.05). We can see that the result shows p-value of much less than
0.05, therefore Normality can be rejected.


   sw_---- <- yield_curve_z %>%
     filter(symbol %in% c('GS2')) %>%
     filter(date >= '2000-01-01') %>%
     select(ret_z) %>%
     pull(ret_z) %>% # extract ret_z values as a numeric vector, which is required by
   shapiro.----()
     shapiro.----()

   print(sw_----)


[EXTRA]: Also we can do a Jarque-Bera ---- to examine if data set has skewness and kurtosis of the
values expected for a Normal distribution. We assume by default (H0, null hypothesis), that the
data is Normally distributed. The alternative belief then is that it is not Normal (H1, alternative

hypothesis). We uphold the null hypothesis unless we can reject it beyond reasonable doubt
(which is if the p-value < 0.05). We can see that the result shows p-value of much less than 0.05,
therefore Normality can be rejected.


   jb_---- <- yield_curve_z %>%
     filter(symbol %in% c('GS2')) %>%
     filter(date >= '2000-01-01') %>%

   jarque.bera.----()
     jarque.bera.----()

   print(jb_----)


[EXTRA]: You could make a check to see which distribution fits your data best. You can do this
with a package called GAMLSS. Fit several distributions to the data and compare them using AIC
(Akaike Information Criterion). The best fit will have the lowest AIC value.


   ret_z_data <- yield_curve_z %>%
     filter(symbol == 'GS2') %>%
     filter(date >= '2000-01-01') %>%
     select(ret_z) %>%
     pull(ret_z) # convert from tibble to a vector

   # Fit different distributions
   fit_normal  <- gamlss(ret_z_data ~ 1, family = NO, trace = FALSE)  # Normal
   fit_t  <- gamlss(ret_z_data ~ 1, family = TF, trace = FALSE)  # t-Distribution
   fit_skewed_t  <- gamlss(ret_z_data ~ 1, family = SST, trace = FALSE) # Skewed t-distribution

   # Compare models using AIC
   models <- list(Normal = fit_normal,
     t_Distribution = fit_t,
     skewed_t = fit_skewed_t)

   # Extract AIC values for comparison
   model_aic <- sapply(models, AIC)
   print(model_aic)

   # Identify the best-fitting distribution
   best_fit <- names(which.min(model_aic))
   print(best_fit)

If we wanted to automatically accept 15% and automatically reject 10%, we are doing the inverse
calculation, namely finding the Z that corresponds to the 85th and 10th percentile, respectively.

Find the z-value that corresponds to the 85th percentile.


   # by default value is TRUE i.e. p(Z<z) = 0.85
   qnorm(0.85, lower.tail = TRUE)
   # if FALSE is used then gives symmetrical value on the other side of the distribution
   qnorm(0.85)

   # But if use FALSE then gives same value as the 15th percentile i.e. P(Z>z) = 0.85
   qnorm(0.85, lower.tail = FALSE)
   qnorm(0.15)


If the mean = 525, and the sd = 55, the X values for automatically accepting 15% and
automatically rejecting 10% of candidates can be found as:


   qnorm(0.85, mean = 525, sd = 55)
   qnorm(0.10, mean = 525, sd = 55)

     degrees_of_freedom = sample_size - 1,

Confidence Intervals

Let's examine movie ratings for different genres.


   movies <- read_csv('movies.csv')
   glimpse(movies)


Choose genres that have at least 5 movies (there are 12 of them)


   genres_to_choose <- movies %>%
     group_by(genre) %>%
     summarise(count = n()) %>%
     filter(count > 5) %>%
     select(genre) %>%
     pull() # creates a vector of characters vs without pull would create a tibble
   # tibble is not an acceptable data type for filtering genre below - you need to
   # specify a vector; if not would get an empty movies tibble)

   glimpse(genres_to_choose)


Plot distributions of ratings, faceted by genre


   movies %>%
     filter(genre %in% genres_to_choose) %>% # genres_to_choose is a vector of genre names
     ggplot(aes(x = rating, colour = genre)) +
     geom_density() +
     facet_wrap(~ genre)+
     theme_bw() +
     theme(legend.position = "none") +
     labs(title = "Distribution of IMDB ratings by film genre",x = "Film Rating",y = " ") +
     NULL


Confidence Interval (CI) using the $point estimate +/- t_{critical} * SE$


   genre_formula_ci <- movies %>%
     filter(genre %in% genres_to_choose) %>%
     group_by(genre) %>%
     summarise(mean_rating = mean(rating),



SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  158

PAGE 159
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 2


     sd_rating = sd(rating),
     count = n(),
     # get t-critical value with (n-1) degrees of freedom
     t_critical = qt(0.975, count-1),  # 95% confidence level
     se_rating = sd(rating) / sqrt(count), # Standard Error
     margin_of_error = t_critical * se_rating,
     rating_low = mean_rating - margin_of_error,
     rating_high = mean_rating + margin_of_error) %>%
     arrange(desc(mean_rating)) # arrange by best mean rating first

   # View CIs for all genres
   print(genre_formula_ci)


Visualise CIs for all genres


   ggplot(genre_formula_ci, aes(x = reorder(genre, mean_rating), y = mean_rating, colour =
   genre)) +
     geom_point() +
     geom_errorbar(width = 0.5, aes(ymin = rating_low, ymax = rating_high)) +
     labs(x = " ",
     y = "Mean IMDB Rating",
     title = "Which film genres have the highest mean IMDB ratings?") +
     theme_bw() +
     coord_flip() +
     theme(legend.position = "none") +
     NULL

  Nomenclature

   Null Hypothesis: H0 belief about true population parameter value Sample mean: H1 alternat‐
   ive

   Significance Level: α α= 5% (corresponds to confidence level 1 − α = 95%) is the probability
   of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true

    Critical value / Cutoff point: z−critical value or t−critical value ±z/t-value which act as cutoff
   points beyond which the null hypothesis should be rejected

    Statistic: z−stat or t−stat standardized value of the sample statistic obtained from the sample

   than, the actual value obtained, when the null hypothesis is true

  What is the null hypothesis in these contexts?

   Court

   H0: The defendant is not guilty

   The defendant is assumed to be not guilty until proven guilty beyond a

   reasonable doubt.

   Production Line

   H0: The machine is in normal condition

   The machine is assumed to be in normal condition until proven abnormal beyond a reasonable
   doubt.

   Drug Approval

   H0: The drug is unsafe

   The drug is assumed to be unsafe until proven to be safe beyond a reasonable doubt.

   Statistical Hypothesis -------

   Hypothesis: is a statement of assertion about the true value of an unknown population
   parameter (e.g. μ= 100).

   Every hypothesis implies its contradiction or an alternative, (e.g. μ≠100).

   The validity of a hypothesis is ------ based on sample data and you may “reject it” or “fail to
   reject it”

  How to report results:

  “we accept the null hypothesis as truth” “we cannot reject the null hypothesis”

   Formulating Hypothesis

          1. The null hypothesis, H0, is assumed to hold unless we obtain significant evidence
        from sample data that suggests otherwise.

          2. The alternative hypothesis, H1, specifies the range of values that excludes the values
         specified by the null.

          3. Hypothesis notation:

   H0: μ= μ0 H1: μ≠μ0





    SOURCE PAGE 9 / 56

  Formulating Hypothesis

   Null Hypothesis is typically:

   Represents the status quo situation or an existing belief. It is typically a:

          1. Value that happened in the past (thus you

   expect it to reoccur)

          2. Value claimed (by a company about their

   product or service)

          3. Value meant to occur e.g. based on regulation (a manufactured item with an
         expectation of a true mean)

   Examples:

          1. Mutual fund was observed to have average annual return of 5%. Null hypothesis could
         state that 5% will continue to be delivered to customers in the future.

          2. Arla Protein Yogurt is claimed to contain an average of 20g of protein per pot. Null
        hypothesis would ---- that claim (i.e. H0: μ= 20).

          3. A blue-chip company makes a forward-looking statement that a $2 dividend is meant
         to occur.

  p-value Approach

   p-value Definition:

        • p-value is the probability of obtaining a value of the ---- statistic (z/t-stat) as extreme
         as, or more extreme than, the actual value obtained from the sample, when the null
        hypothesis is true

        • p-value gives the probability of observing the ---- statistic (z/t-stat) if the hypothesis
       was true.

   Significance level is the minimum p-value that we allow if the hypothesis was true (e.g. α=
  5%)

   Example:

        • If we found z-stat = -2.5, we can mark this on the Normal distribution as before, and
          find the probability P(Z< −2.5) + P(Z> 2.5) which in total equals to the p-value.

   Standard Normal distribution if using z-statistic

PAGE 175
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 3


   (t-distribution if using t-statistic)

  more extreme than -2.5

  more extreme than 2.5
