  Hypothesis ------- with p-value

   p-value Calculation Steps:

   Step1: Calculate the z/t-stat using the formula (use σ if

   x̄−μ0

     it is known):

   s n

   Step 2: Calculate the total probability in the tails to the left and right of the z/t-stat using a
   function in R

   Step 3: Compare the total probability (also known as the p-value, e.g. p= 1.2%) with the
   significance level (e.g. α= 5%)

   Step 4: Decision, reject H0 if the p-value < α

   Surprising:

  p< 0.05

  2.5% 2.5%

   Not surprising:

  p> 0.05

  95%





    SOURCE PAGE 28 / 56

  p-value Calculation

   Using R obtain the tail probability to the left of the negative statistic and multiply it by 2, since
   this probability is equal in both tails by symmetry.

  We formulate a general syntax, that always uses notation –abs() to avoid mistakes:

   p-value Calculation for z-stat: p <- 2 * mosaic::xpnorm(abs(z_statistic))

   p-value Calculation for t-stat: p <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_statistic), n-1)

   p-value CVR Example:

  p-value Approach: Overall Steps

          1. Write down the hypothesis

   H0: μ= μ0 H1: μ≠μ0

          2. Choose significance level, typically α= 5%

          3. Decide if you are using z or t-distribution and

   x̄−μ0

   calculate z/t-statistic using formula:

   SE

          4. Use R to calculate p-value as:

        • If using z-statistic, the p-value is: p <- 2 * mosaic::xpnorm(-abs(z_stat))

        • If using t-statistic, the p-value is: p <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_stat), n-1)

          5. Make a decision:

        • If p-value < 0.05 reject the null hypothesis, the result is significant.

        • If p-value > 0.05 cannot reject the null

   hypothesis.

  We have 3 equivalent ways of ------- hypothesis. The decision taken based on one approach will
   agree with the rest, therefore you only need to use a single approach (recommended
   approach: p-value).

   Approach Decision Rule Calculation


      Approach (1) Confidence Interval (CI built around x̄) Confidence Interval (CI built around
      μ0)

     x̄ ± z


      n (use z, or t)*


   s

      n (use z, or t)*



      Approach (2) t-statistic z-statistic

   For α= 5% use t = qt(0.975, n-1) For α= 5% use z = qnorm(0.975)


      Approach (3) p-value (find probability for t-stat) Reject H0 if p< α Typical α:

   The difference between two sample means can be due to a real difference between true mean
   parameters of the groups (significant difference) or due to the inherent randomness in the
   sampling process (sampling error).

  When can we conclude there is a difference in true means?

   Start with the theory there is no difference, then try to disprove it by finding significant
   evidence from data.

   For 2 groups:

   Group 1 Group 2

   μ1, σ1 μ2, σ2

   Formulate the hypothesis as:

   H0: μ1 −μ2 = 0 H1: μ1 −μ2 ≠0





    SOURCE PAGE 37 / 56

   ------- for Differences: CI Approach

   Build a joint confidence interval Take a random sample from each population of size n1 and n2,
   respectively (unequal sample sizes is ok).

   Calculate sample means x̄1 and x̄2 and obtain their difference x̄1 −x̄2.

   Null hypothesis: no difference between population means (μ1 = μ2) i.e. samples are drawn
   from 2 populations with the same mean.

   Establish sampling distribution of differences in means approx. Normally distributed by CLT if
  n> 30 or tdistributed if group populations are Normal, standard deviations are unknown and
  n< 30

    Joint CI Calculation Assume n is large, then by CLT we can use z-value.

   The standard error is:

   Replace with σ1 and σ2 if they are known.

   SE x̄1 −x̄2 = s12

  + s22

  n1

  n2

   The 95% Confidence Interval for the difference between means is:

   Use z= 2 as approxim ation

    ( x̄1−x̄2) ± zs12

  + s22

    SOURCE PAGE 41 / 56

   ------- for Differences Mean Movie Ratings

  When comparing means we do not care about differences in individual values. For example, in
   Biography vs. Horror, there can be an individual horror movie that has a higher rating than a
   Bio movie. We care whether the population mean rating between groups is the same or not.

    SOURCE PAGE 49 / 56

  Types of Statistical Errors

   Because of the potential for extreme sampling error, two possible errors can occur when a hy‐
   pothesis is ------: Type I and Type II errors. These errors show the relationship between what ac‐
   tually exists (a state of nature) and the decision made based on the sample information.





    SOURCE PAGE 50 / 56

  Type I vs Type II Errors

   Type I Error:

  α = P(reject a true null ℎypotℎesis)

  α is the probability of making a Type I Error!

   H0: not pregnant H1: pregnant

   False Positive: concluding something exists when it doesn’t

   Type II Error:

  β = P(fail to reject a false null ℎypotℎesis)

   H0: not pregnant H1: pregnant

   False Negative: concluding there is no effect when there is; i.e. missing a true positive





    SOURCE PAGE 51 / 56

  What is the effect of the significance level on hypothesis -------?

  95% Confidence: (α= 5%) z-critical value 1.96

   Say you had a t-statistic = 1.876

  90% Confidence: (α= 10%) z-critical value 1.64

    t-stat = 1.876 t-stat = 1.876

  95%

  2.5% 2.5% 5% 5%

    -1. 96 +1. 96 -1. 64 +1. 64

   |1.876| < 1.96, therefore we would not reject H0.

   |1.876| > 1.64, therefore we would reject H0.

  A smaller Confidence Level (larger α) leads to a more precise but less confident result (higher
    risk, 10%, of rejecting a true null hypothesis).

  90%

    SOURCE PAGE 53 / 56

  Industry Conventions for α

   Conventions in Your Industry:

   Psychology / education α= 0.05 Good balance of avoiding false positives and detecting
   genuine effects.

   Physics / chemistry α= 0.001 Stricter threshold ensures extremely robust findings, i.e. assume
   your idea is not correct and let the evidence reject this null.

   Marketing / finance α= 0.1 Typically, data has inherent noise. Larger α means we will reject
   the null hypothesis more often thus giving us a greater chance of detecting potential trends
  among noise. Missing a true positive (Type II error) could mean missing an important business
   opportunity.

   Examples:

   H0: μnew teacℎing metℎod−μold teacℎing metℎod= 0 H1: μnew teacℎing metℎod−μold
   teacℎing metℎod≠0

   H0: μ= μtℎere is no life on tℎe moon H1: μ≠μtℎere is life on tℎe moon

   H0: μsales after advertising−μsales before advertising= 0 H1: μsales after advertising−μsales
   before advertising≠0

  What α Shall I Pick?

   General Convention:

   Factors that influence choice of significance level:

   Significance Level (α) is the probability of rejecting a null hypothesis when it is true.

   Sample Size and Variance





SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  188

PAGE 189
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 3


        • More Stable Results happen when: you have large sample size and low variance Use a
        lower significance level to α= 0.01 to increase the confidence in your results, i.e. setting
          stricter threshold for declaring significance (reject less often)

   Standard choice of alpha is 5% (α = 0.05) is commonly used across many fields.

   There are some factors that may influence your choice of the significance level.

        • More Unstable Results happen when: you have small sample size and high variance
       Use a higher significance level to 10% (α= 0.1) i.e. more willing to detect significance
          (reject more often)

  Nomenclature

   Null Hypothesis: H0 belief about true population parameter value Sample mean: H1 alternat‐
   ive

   Significance Level: α α= 5% (corresponds to confidence level 1 − α = 95%) is the probability
   of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true

    Critical value / Cutoff point: z−critical value or t−critical value ±z/t-value which act as cutoff
   points beyond which the null hypothesis should be rejected

    Statistic: z−stat or t−stat standardized value of the sample statistic obtained from the sample

   p-value: p probability of obtaining a value of the ---- statistic as extreme as, or more extreme
   than, the actual value obtained, when the null hypothesis is true

  What is the null hypothesis in these contexts?

   Court

   H0: The defendant is not guilty

   The defendant is assumed to be not guilty until proven guilty beyond a

   reasonable doubt.

   Production Line

   H0: The machine is in normal condition

   The machine is assumed to be in normal condition until proven abnormal beyond a reasonable
   doubt.

   Drug Approval

   H0: The drug is unsafe

   The drug is assumed to be unsafe until proven to be safe beyond a reasonable doubt.

    SOURCE PAGE 8 / 62

   Statistical Hypothesis -------

   Hypothesis: is a statement of assertion about the true value of an unknown population
   parameter (e.g. μ= 100).

   Every hypothesis implies its contradiction or an alternative, (e.g. μ≠100).

   The validity of a hypothesis is ------ based on sample data and you may “reject it” or “fail to
   reject it”

  How to report results:

  “we accept the null hypothesis as truth” “we cannot reject the null hypothesis”

   Formulating Hypothesis

          1. The null hypothesis, H0, is assumed to hold unless we obtain significant evidence
        from sample data that suggests otherwise.

          2. The alternative hypothesis, H1, specifies the range of values that excludes the values
         specified by the null.

          3. Hypothesis notation:

   H0: μ= μ0 H1: μ≠μ0





    SOURCE PAGE 9 / 62

  Formulating Hypothesis

   Null Hypothesis is typically:

   Represents the status quo situation or an existing belief. It is typically a:

          1. Value that happened in the past (thus you

   expect it to reoccur)

          2. Value claimed (by a company about their

   product or service)

          3. Value meant to occur e.g. based on regulation (a manufactured item with an
         expectation of a true mean)

   Examples:

          1. Mutual fund was observed to have average annual return of 5%. Null hypothesis could
         state that 5% will continue to be delivered to customers in the future.

          2. Arla Protein Yogurt is claimed to contain an average of 20g of protein per pot. Null
        hypothesis would ---- that claim (i.e. H0: μ= 20).

          3. A blue-chip company makes a forward-looking statement that a $2 dividend is meant
         to occur.

   Perform a hypothesis ---- based on past values.

  Hypothesis -------: CI Approach

   Null hypothesis: H0: μ= μ0

        • Claims a value for population mean Alternative hypothesis: H1: μ≠μ0

        • Population mean does not equal the claim

   Hypothesis ------- Idea:

          1. Assume hypothesized mean μ0 is true

          2. Form CI around μ0 (i.e. obtain cutoff points: upper and lower CI bounds)

          3. Examine whether the sample mean falls within the formed CI

          4. If it does, do not reject the null hypothesis

   Most likely values of x̄, given null hypothesis is correct

  μ0 − z s

   n μ0 + z s

   n

   Construct CI around μ0

          1. Form a 95% CI around the claim μ0. For CVR example, n> 30 therefore CLT holds, and
      we use the z-value:

   C.I.= μ0 ± 1.96 s

   n = 0.3 ± 0.0788 = [0.22, 0.38]

          3. Check if sample mean is contained inside the CI

   Decision:

  p-value Approach

   p-value Definition:

        • p-value is the probability of obtaining a value of the ---- statistic (z/t-stat) as extreme
         as, or more extreme than, the actual value obtained from the sample, when the null
        hypothesis is true

        • p-value gives the probability of observing the ---- statistic (z/t-stat) if the hypothesis
       was true.

   Significance level is the minimum p-value that we allow if the hypothesis was true (e.g. α=
  5%)

   Example:

        • If we found z-stat = -2.5, we can mark this on the Normal distribution as before, and
          find the probability P(Z < −2.5) + P(Z> 2.5) which in total equals to the p-value.

   Standard Normal distribution if using z-statistic

   (t-distribution if using t-statistic)

  more extreme than -2.5

  more extreme than 2.5

   function in R

   Step 3: Compare the total probability (also known as the p-value, e.g. p= 1.2%) with the
   significance level (e.g. α = 5%)

   Step 4: Decision, reject H0 if the p-value < α

  p-value Calculation

   Using R obtain the tail probability to the left of the negative statistic and multiply it by 2, since
   this probability is equal in both tails by symmetry.

  We formulate a general syntax, that always uses notation –abs() to avoid mistakes:

   p-value Calculation for z-stat: p <- 2 * mosaic::xpnorm(abs(z_statistic))

   p-value Calculation for t-stat: p <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_statistic), n-1)

   p-value CVR Example:

  We use z-stat since n=100 is >30. Hence:

   z −stat= x̄−μ0

  2 x

  p-value Approach: Overall Steps

          1. Write down the hypothesis

   H0: μ= μ0 H1: μ≠μ0

          2. Choose significance level, typically α= 5%

          3. Decide if you are using z or t-distribution and

   x̄−μ0

   calculate z/t-statistic using formula:

   SE

          4. Use R to calculate p-value as:

        • If using z-statistic, the p-value is: p <- 2 * mosaic::xpnorm(-abs(z_stat))

        • If using t-statistic, the p-value is: p <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_stat), n-1)

          5. Make a decision:

        • If p-value < 0.05 reject the null hypothesis, the result is significant.

        • If p-value > 0.05 cannot reject the null

   hypothesis.

  Decision Rule Summary

  We have 3 equivalent ways of ------- hypothesis. The decision taken based on one approach will
   agree with the rest, therefore you only need to use a single approach (recommended
   approach: p-value).

   Approach Decision Rule Calculation


      Approach (1) Confidence Interval (CI built around x̄) Confidence Interval (CI built around
      μ0)


   Reject H0 if claim (μ0) is outside CI Reject H0 if evidence ( x̄) is outside CI

   s

     x̄ ± z


      n (use z, or t)*


   s

  μ0 ± z


      n (use z, or t)*



      Approach (2) t-statistic z-statistic


   Reject H0 if |t-stat| > critical level t Reject H0 if |z-stat| > critical level z

   For α= 5% use t = qt(0.975, n-1) For α= 5% use z = qnorm(0.975)


      Approach (3) p-value (find probability for t-stat) Reject H0 if p< α Typical α:


   0.01 1% , 0.05 5% , 0.10(10%)

   For α= 5% use p=2*pt(-abs(tstat),n-1)

   For ----: use t if n< 30, population distribution is Normal, and σ is unknown. Otherwise, use z.

   But! in practice we always use t since the t-distribution converges to Standard Normal as
   sample size increases. For ----: for 95% confidence level (i.e. 5% critical level) use z= 1.96 or
   round up to z= 2.

  Motivation

   Examples of ------- for Differences

        • Difference between true mean of two stocks

        • Difference in true mean sales volume of two agents

        • Difference in true mean salaries between different

   groups of employees

   The difference between two sample means can be due to a real difference between true mean
   parameters of the groups (significant difference) or due to the inherent randomness in the
   sampling process (sampling error).

  When can we conclude there is a difference in true means?

   Start with the theory there is no difference, then try to disprove it by finding significant
   evidence from data.

   For 2 groups:

   Group 1 Group 2

   μ1, σ1 μ2, σ2

   Formulate the hypothesis as:

   H0: μ1 −μ2 = 0 H1: μ1 −μ2 ≠0





    SOURCE PAGE 42 / 62

   ------- for Differences: CI Approach

   Build a joint confidence interval Take a random sample from each population of size n1 and n2,
   respectively (unequal sample sizes is ok).

   Calculate sample means x̄1 and x̄2 and obtain their difference x̄1 −x̄2.

   Null hypothesis: no difference between population means (μ1 = μ2) i.e. samples are drawn
   from 2 populations with the same mean.

   Establish sampling distribution of differences in means approx. Normally distributed by CLT if
  n> 30 or tdistributed if group populations are Normal, standard deviations are unknown and
  n< 30

    Joint CI Calculation Assume n is large, then by CLT we can use z-value.

   The standard error is:

   Replace with σ1 and σ2 if they are known.

   SE x̄1 −x̄2 = s12

  + s22

  n1

  n2

   The 95% Confidence Interval for the difference between means is:

   Use z = 2 as approxim ation

    ( x̄1−x̄2) ± zs12

  + s22

  n1

  n2

   Decision rule: if the joint CI does not contain 0, then reject the null, H0.

  Types of Statistical Errors

   Because of the potential for extreme sampling error, two possible errors can occur when a hy‐
   pothesis is ------: Type I and Type II errors. These errors show the relationship between what ac‐
   tually exists (a state of nature) and the decision made based on the sample information.





    SOURCE PAGE 56 / 62

  Type I vs Type II Errors

   Type I Error:

  α = P(reject a true null ℎypotℎesis)

  α is the probability of making a Type I Error!

   H0: not pregnant H1: pregnant

   False Positive: concluding something exists when it doesn’t

   Type II Error:

  β = P(fail to reject a false null ℎypotℎesis)

   H0: not pregnant H1: pregnant

   False Negative: concluding there is no effect when there is; i.e. missing a true positive





    SOURCE PAGE 57 / 62

  What is the effect of the significance level on hypothesis -------?

  95% Confidence: (α= 5%) z-critical value 1.96

   Say you had a t-statistic = 1.876

  90% Confidence: (α= 10%) z-critical value 1.64

    t-stat = 1.876 t-stat = 1.876

  95%

  2.5% 2.5% 5% 5%

    -1. 96 +1. 96 -1. 64 +1. 64

   |1.876| < 1.96, therefore we would not reject H0.

   |1.876| > 1.64, therefore we would reject H0.

  A smaller Confidence Level (larger α) leads to a more precise but less confident result (higher
    risk, 10%, of rejecting a true null hypothesis).

  90%

   17.2 19.6

    SOURCE PAGE 59 / 62

  Industry Conventions for α

   Conventions in Your Industry:

   Psychology / education α= 0.05 Good balance of avoiding false positives and detecting
   genuine effects.

   Physics / chemistry α= 0.001 Stricter threshold ensures extremely robust findings, i.e. assume
   your idea is not correct and let the evidence reject this null.

   Marketing / finance α= 0.1 Typically, data has inherent noise. Larger α means we will reject
   the null hypothesis more often thus giving us a greater chance of detecting potential trends
  among noise. Missing a true positive (Type II error) could mean missing an important business
   opportunity.

   Examples:

   H0: μnew teacℎing metℎod−μold teacℎing metℎod= 0 H1: μnew teacℎing metℎod−μold
   teacℎing metℎod≠0

   H0: μ= μtℎere is no life on tℎe moon H1: μ≠μtℎere is life on tℎe moon

   H0: μsales after advertising−μsales before advertising= 0 H1: μsales after advertising−μsales
   before advertising≠0





    SOURCE PAGE 60 / 62

  False Positives vs False Negatives

   https://www.theguardian.com/society/article/2024/jun/23/dwp-algorithm-wrongly-
   flags-200000-people-possible-fraud-error https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/07/18/
   technology/spain-domestic-violence-viogen-algorithm.html





    SOURCE PAGE 61 / 62

  What α Shall I Pick?

   General Convention:

   Factors that influence choice of significance level:

   Significance Level (α) is the probability of rejecting a null hypothesis when it is true.

   Sample Size and Variance





SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  218

PAGE 219
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 3


        • More Stable Results happen when: you have large sample size and low variance Use a
        lower significance level to α= 0.01 to increase the confidence in your results, i.e. setting
          stricter threshold for declaring significance (reject less often)

   Standard choice of alpha is 5% (α = 0.05) is commonly used across many fields.

   There are some factors that may influence your choice of the significance level.

        • More Unstable Results happen when: you have small sample size and high variance
       Use a higher significance level to 10% (α= 0.1) i.e. more willing to detect significance
          (reject more often)

Hypothesis -------

Conversion Rate Exercise


   cvr <- read_csv('CVR.csv')
   mu0 <- 0.3 # this is the null hypothesis

   stats <- cvr %>%
     summarise(mu0 = 0.3,
     xbar = mean(conversion),
     s = sd(conversion),
     n = n(),
     # get z-critical value
     z_critical = qnorm(0.975), # 95% confidence level
     SE = s / sqrt(n), # Standard Error
     margin_of_error = z_critical * SE,
     CI_low = mu0 - margin_of_error,
     CI_high = mu0 + margin_of_error)
   print(stats)


Hypothesis ------- CVR, three approaches:

CONFIDENCE INTERVAL APPROACH (A)

Building confidence interval around sample mean.


   upper_CI <- stats$xbar + stats$z_critical * (stats$s/sqrt(stats$n)) # 0.28
   lower_CI <- stats$xbar - stats$z_critical * (stats$s/sqrt(stats$n)) # 0.12
   # Since mu0 = 0.30 is outside the interval we reject the null hypothesis





SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  220

PAGE 221
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 3


CONFIDENCE INTERVAL APPROACH (B)

Building confidence interval around claimed mean.


   upper_CI <- mu0 + stats$z_critical * (stats$s/sqrt(stats$n)) # 0.38
   lower_CI <- mu0 - stats$z_critical * (stats$s/sqrt(stats$n)) # 0.22
   # Since xbar = 0.20 is outside the interval we reject the null hypothesis


Z-STAT APPROACH


   z_stat <- (stats$xbar - mu0) / stats$SE  # -2.487 (approx -2.5)
   reject_t <- abs(z_stat) > stats$z_critical # TRUE
   # Since z-stat in abs value is greater than critical level, we reject the null hypothesis


P-VALUE APPROACH


   p_value <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z_stat)) # 0.013
   reject_p <- p_value < 0.05  # TRUE
   # Since p-value is less than 0.05 we reject the null hypothesis


AUTOMATE HYPOTHESIS ------- WITH T.----()

In practice we use the t-distribution.


   options(digits = 5)
   t.----(cvr$conversion, mu = 0.3, data = cvr)


Reproducing Plots from the Slides

Plot with coloured 95% of the density.


   # Generate a sequence of x values for the standard normal distribution
   data <- data.frame(x = seq(-4, 4, by = 0.01))

   # Calculate the density of the standard normal distribution
   data <- data %>%
     mutate(y = dnorm(x),
     # Identify whether each point falls within the 95% interval
     in_interval = ifelse(x >= -1.96 & x <= 1.96, TRUE, FALSE))

   # Plot the standard normal distribution
   ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
     geom_line(color = "black") +  # Plot the normal distribution line
     geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = 0, ymax = ifelse(in_interval, y, NA)), fill = "green", alpha = 0.5) +
   # Shade the 95% interval
     labs(title = "Standard Normal Distribution with 95% Confidence Interval",
     x = "Z-score",
     y = "Density") +
     theme_minimal() +
     theme(
     axis.text.x = element_text(size = 16),  # Set x-axis tick font size
     axis.text.y = element_text(size = 16),  # Set y-axis tick font size
     axis.title.x = element_text(size = 18), # Set x-axis label font size
     axis.title.y = element_text(size = 18), # Set y-axis label font size

   # Confidence Interval (CI) using the formula mean +- t_critical * SE
   genre_formula_ci <- movies %>%
     filter (genre %in% c("Crime", "Drama", "Action", "Comedy")) %>%
     group_by(genre) %>%
     summarise(mean_rating = mean(rating),
     sd_rating = sd(rating),
     count = n(),
     # get t-critical value with (n-1) degrees of freedom
     t_critical = qt(0.975, count-1),
     se_rating = sd(rating) / sqrt(count),
     margin_of_error = t_critical * se_rating,
     rating_low = mean_rating - margin_of_error,
     rating_high = mean_rating + margin_of_error) %>%
     arrange(desc(mean_rating))

   print(genre_formula_ci)



   # Visualise CIs for 4 genres.
   ggplot(genre_formula_ci, aes(x = reorder(genre, mean_rating), y = mean_rating, colour =
   genre)) +
     geom_point() +
     geom_errorbar(width = 0.2, aes(ymin = rating_low, ymax = rating_high)) +
     labs(x =" ",
     y = "Mean IMDB Rating",
     title = "Which film genres have the highest mean IMDB ratings?") +
     theme_bw() +
     coord_flip() +
     theme(legend.position = "none") +

  Correlation Definition

   Correlation: is a numerical measure of a degree of linear relationship between two variables X
   and Y.

        • X interest rates and Y bond prices

        • X GDP and Y stock prices

        • X crude oil prices and Y airline stock prices

    (-) (+)

    (-)

   Sample Correlation Coefficient (r): is a common correlation measure.

   In R, use function cor(X,Y).

   Correlation Properties

        • Range: −1 ≤ rxy≤+1

        • It is symmetrical: rxy= ryx

        • It does not imply causation, only association

        • Unitless measure

        • Sensitive to outliers

   Degree of strength Range Perfect |r| = 1 Very strong

          0. 9≤|r| < 1. 0 Strong

          0. 7≤|r| < 0. 9 Moderate

          0. 5≤|r| < 0. 7 Weak

          0. 3≤|r| < 0. 5 Negligible 0≤|r| < 0. 3





    SOURCE PAGE 8 / 59

  Correlation Illustration

   Negative Correlation: increasing values in one variable are associated with decreasing values
   of the other.

   Positive Correlation: increasing values of one variable are associated with increasing values of
   the other.

   rxy= +1 indicates a perfect positive linear relationship rxy= −1 indicates a perfect decreasing
   linear relationship rxy= 0 indicates no linear relationship −1 < rxy< 0 indicates a decreasing
   linear relationship 0 < rxy< 1 indicates a positive linear relationship





    SOURCE PAGE 9 / 59

  Anscombe’s quartet

   Anscombe’s quartet is a dataframe with 4 datasets, each with n = 11 datapoints, and all
   datasets have the same mean and standard deviation for both x and y.

   Would you expect to have any differences among the data in the 4 datasets? After all, they all
   have the same mean, sd, and cor(x, y).





    SOURCE PAGE 10 / 59

  Anscombe’s quartet

   Even though the correlation coefficients are identical, data has different distributions and are
   very different when plotted.

        • Correlation does not reflect nonlinear relationships.

        • Correlation coefficient is sensitive to outliers.

  Correlation Interpretation

  Remember: correlation measures only the degree of linear relationships!

   Correlation reflects noisiness and direction of a linear relationship.

   Correlation does not reflect the slope of a linear relationship.

   Correlation does not reflect nonlinear relationships.

    SOURCE PAGE 13 / 59

  Correlation vs Causation

   Shoe sizes vs. Grades:

   Consider elementary school --------' shoe sizes and scores on a standard reading ----. They are
   correlated but saying that larger shoe size causes higher reading scores is as absurd.

   Ice cream sales vs Shark attacks:

   Ice cream sales correlate with shark attacks. So are some types of crime rates in certain areas.
   But you cannot reduce shark attacks or crime by reducing the consumption of ice cream.

   Confounding/Lurking/Common Response Variable

  A typical reason for why variables are correlated but do not have a causal relationship is a
   confounding variable that creates a spurious (false) correlation.

   Confound variable is an external variable / factor that influences both X and Y variables thus
   making it seem like there is a statistical relationship between X and Y, but it is caused by a
   third variable.

   e.g. older -------- had more practice with ----- and -------- thus do better e.g. due to it being the
  summer time more swimmers are in the water

  London Cholera Outbreaks in the 1850s

  miasma or ‘bad air’: Bad smells given off by waste and rotting matter and believed to be the
   main source of cholera

   Source: John Leech's cartoon in Punch, 23 (25 September 1852): 139 http://www.victorian‐
   web.org/science/health/cholera/cholera.html





    SOURCE PAGE 15 / 59

  John Snow

   John Snow is regarded as one of the founding fathers of modern epidemiology who believed
   that cholera spread through contaminated water. This contradicted the prevailing theory that
   diseases were spread by miasma in the air.

   The September 1854 cholera outbreak was centered in the Soho district, close to Snow's
   house. Snow mapped the 13 public wells and all the known cholera deaths around Soho, and
   noted the spatial clustering of cases around one particular water pump on the southwest
   corner of the intersection of Broad (now Broadwick) Street and Cambridge (now Lexington)
   Street.

  He examined water samples from various wells under a microscope, and confirmed the pres‐
   ence of an unknown bacterium in the Broad Street samples. Despite strong scepticism from
   the local authorities, he had the pump handle removed from the Broad Street pump and the
   outbreak quickly subsided.

   Causality can be inferred from random assignment: If the treatment and control groups are
   similar apart from the treatment, then differences between the outcomes in the two groups
   can be ascribed to the treatment.

  Modeling

   Analyzing Individual Variables So far, we have analyzed individual variables by forming
   confidence intervals and hypothesis -------.

   Analyzing Relationships Between Variables Next, we will analyze relationships between one or
  more variables. Our goal is to build models with explanatory power to predict performance.

   Applications:

        • Understanding factors that drive financial index/ ETF performance

        • Forecast investment return or business sales

  Why Analyze Relationships?

   In Finance we want to know how are stock prices affected by market movements?

  What is the impact of mergers on stockholder’s value?

   In Marketing, how affective are different type of advertising?

  Do promotions simply shift sales without affecting the overall volume?

   In Economics how do interest rates affect consumer behavior?

  How do trade policies influence imports/exports?

    SOURCE PAGE 25 / 59

  Two Purposes of Regression

   Statistics / Econometrics: you should have theoretical reason to include each variable in your
   equation.

   Machine Learning: automatic selection of the best independent variables from the ones
   provided.

   Prediction Explanation Focus on Y Focus on x Predict the future Explain effect of x on Y

   You try to make the best prediction of Y e.g. Predicting the price of a used Prius e.g. Netflix
   trying to guess your next show

   You try to explain the effect that specific variables, x′s, have on Y e.g. Looking at the effect of
   mileage on the price of a used Prius e.g. Netflix looking at the effect of time of day on show
   selection

  Estimates of Residual Errors

  We want to make the residuals:

  We can visualize residuals using a Residual Error Plot.

          1. Have an average of zero (this is equivalent to saying ‘there is no bias’)

          2. Be “as small as possible” (by minimizing the squares of the errors with respect to
          coefficients). This is equivalent to saying “we want to minimize the standard deviation of
        the residual errors”.

          2. p-values of the coefficients

          3. Standard error of the regression residuals

          4. R-squared





    SOURCE PAGE 37 / 59

  Significance of Coefficients

  We have found the coefficients of the equation:

   ෢ criminalsi= መβ0 + መβ1 ∗pubsi

   Rule is:

        • Always keep the intercept in the equation as it allows the regression line to not be
         fixed at the origin

        • Decide if coefficient of the x variable is significantly different from 0.

   Q: Why do we need to decide that?





    SOURCE PAGE 38 / 59

  Significance of Coefficients

  We have found the coefficients of the equation:

   ෢ criminalsi= መβ0 + መβ1 ∗pubsi

     If መβ1 = 0, then pubs has no influence on criminals since the equation becomes: ෢ criminalsi=
   መβ0.

   Let’s establish whether the public_houses variable has predictive power on the crime variable
   at α= 5%.

   Hypothesis ------- for Regression Coefficients H0: መβ1 = 0 implies no relationship between x
   and Y H1: መβ1 ≠0 coefficient is significant

        • Since the public_houses p-value 0.0026 < 0.05 we can reject H0 and conclude the
          coefficient is significant.

        • Alternatively, you can base your decision on the t-stat, since |3.22| > 2, reject the null
         hypothesis.

   Therefore, pubs does have predictive power on crime and we can write down the equation of
   regression line:

   ෢ criminalsi= 109.34 + 0.1162 ∗pubsi





    SOURCE PAGE 39 / 59

  Point Prediction and Prediction Interval

   Valid Model: all coefficients are significant (except the intercept which we always keep).

  Once we ensure the model is valid, we can write down the equation of the fitted regression
    line as:

   ෢ criminalsi= 109.34 + 0.1162 ∗pubsi

   This equation can be used to make a point prediction. A single-valued estimate of ෢Yt for a
   given value of xt is obtained by inserting the value of xt:

   ෢ criminalsi= 109.34 + 0.1162 ∗72 = 117.98

   However, how certain are we about this value?

   Prediction Interval Use the residual standard error to form approximate prediction interval for
   ෢Yt for the given value of xt.

   ෢Yt± 1.96 ∗S

   Example: for xt= 72, ෢Yt= 117.98, the interval is:

   117.98 1.96 ∗37.2 = [45.07, 190.89]

  Residual Standard Error

   Residual Standard Error (RSE) is the square root of the average squared residuals:

   n yi−ොyi2

  RSE= se= σi=1

  n−p−1




SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  241

PAGE 242
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 4


   where n is the number of observations and p number of independent variables.

   Importance of RSE:

   Measure of Model Accuracy: how well model predicts the observed data (smaller se means
   better line fit).

   Comparison: compare the fit of different models by selecting the one with the smaller se

   Model Adequacy: compare RSE to standard deviation of the dependent variable (if se ≫σY
   then model is not capturing the data patterns well).





    SOURCE PAGE 42 / 59

  R2

   Coefficient of Determination, R2 = corr2 describes ‘goodness of fit’ of a regression model i.e.
  how well does the line fit the data?

        • Model is never perfect

        • Model captures part of the variability of the data

  R2 = 1 line fits the data perfectly R2 = 0 model explains none of the variability in Y

     It is calculated as:

   σ ෢Yi−തY

  R2 = Explained Variation

   σ Yi−തY2 = corr2

   Total Variation =

  2 is the variance of the fitted ෢Yi points and σ Yi−തY2 is the variance of the original Y points

   where σ ෢Yi−തY

   Interpretation of R2

        • R2 shows how much better your model is compared to the unconditional forecast
         (naïve model) that predicts every value of Y to be the mean(Y)?

   n yi n−1

   ෢Yt= തY= σi=1

        • R2 shows the proportion of total variation of Y that is explained by the model (i.e. by
        the independent variable(s))

  R2

   The higher the R2 the greater the explanatory power of the model.





    SOURCE PAGE 44 / 59

  Adjusted R2

   Adjusted R2

   Adjusts the R2 statistic for the number of independent variables present in the model.

        • As the number of inputs (x’s) increases, R2 typically increases regardless of whether
        the variables are useful for prediction.

        • Adjusted R2 will only increase if the new x variable improves the model more than
        would be expected by chance.

  = 1 −(n−1)

  n−p−1 1 −R2

   Radj

   where n is the number of observations and p number of independent variables. If n is very
   large and p is very small, the ratio is close to zero, and R2 ≈Radj

   Negative Adj R2:

   which means that the model fits worse than the naïve model.

     It is possible to have negative values of Radj

     It can happen because:

        • No intercept was used (forcing the line to go through origin doesn’t make sense for
       many real-life tasks)

        • Overfitting (great performance on training data with

   but poor out-of-sample prediction with

   high Radj

    )

   low/negative Radj

   Model Selection:

  When selecting among competing models, select the one where all variables are significant,
   the model has the largest Adj R2, and smallest RSE.

    SOURCE PAGE 49 / 59

  Linear Regression Model Assumptions

   Assumptions:

   [A1] Relationship between x and Y is linear.

   [A2] Randomness in Y values comes purely from the error term ε. Values of the independent
   variable x are assumed fixed and not random.

   [A3] Errors are uncorrelated with independent variables, x.

   [A4] Errors are uncorrelated with each other in successive observations i.e. errors are
   independent of each other.

   Assumptions:

   [A5] Errors are Normally distributed with mean 0 and variance σ2, ε~N(0, σ2). Note: constant,
   time independent variance is called homoscedasticity.

   ε~N(0, σ2) assumption is essential for:

        • Hypothesis ------- of regression coefficients.

        • Interval estimation around point prediction.



SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  245

PAGE 246
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 4


        • Model validity: “are residuals Normally distributed?” ➢Normal residuals: model cor‐
          rectly specified ➢Nonnormal residuals: nonlinearity present, interactions between
        independent variables, outliers

  How Residuals Should Look

  Random scatter with no visible pattern.

   Constant variance of the residuals





    SOURCE PAGE 51 / 59

  Regression Error Analysis

  We should not be making systematic errors.

   Systematic error: means errors exhibit some consistent, non-random pattern, rather than
   being distributed randomly around the regression line.

   Systematic error presence means regression model is not fully capturing the relationship
   between Y and x’s.

  Any systematic component should be in the model rather than in the error.

  By including the systematic error in the model, the model should improve.

   outcomei= modeli+ errori

    yi

    xi Systematic part

    εi Unsystematic part

   Possible Reasons For Systematic Errors:

        • Nonlinearity: systematic pattern in the residuals

        • Heteroscedasticity: variance of errors changes across levels of independent variable

        • Autocorrelation: errors in one period are correlated

   with errors in another period





    SOURCE PAGE 52 / 59

  Systematic Errors: Autocorrelation

   Serial correlation / autocorrelation: means errors are correlated with each other over time. It
   violates the assumption of independence of errors.

   The residual plot shows a clear linear pattern.

   You may also see a wave-like or cyclical pattern.

   Remedy: introduce lags.

   Example:

   ෢ Salest= ොa+ ෢bAdvertisingt+ ƸcAdvertisingt−1

  Correlation Definition

   Correlation: is a numerical measure of a degree of linear relationship between two variables X
   and Y.

        • X interest rates and Y bond prices

        • X GDP and Y stock prices

        • X crude oil prices and Y airline stock prices

    (-) (+)

    (-)

   Sample Correlation Coefficient (r): is a common correlation measure.

   In R, use function cor(X,Y).

   Correlation Properties

        • Range: −1 ≤ rxy≤+1

        • It is symmetrical: rxy= ryx

        • It does not imply causation, only association

        • Sensitive to outliers

          0. 9≤|r| < 1. 0 Strong

          0. 7≤|r| < 0. 9 Moderate

          0. 5≤|r| < 0. 7 Weak

          0. 3≤|r| < 0. 5 Negligible 0≤|r| < 0. 3





    SOURCE PAGE 8 / 64

  Correlation Illustration

   Negative Correlation: increasing values in one variable are associated with decreasing values
   of the other.

   Positive Correlation: increasing values of one variable are associated with increasing values of
   the other.

   rxy= +1 indicates a perfect positive linear relationship rxy= −1 indicates a perfect decreasing
   linear relationship rxy= 0 indicates no linear relationship −1 < rxy< 0 indicates a decreasing
   linear relationship 0 < rxy< 1 indicates a positive linear relationship

  Anscombe’s quartet

   Anscombe’s quartet is a dataframe with 4 datasets, each with n = 11 datapoints, and all
   datasets have the same mean and standard deviation for both x and y.

   Would you expect to have any differences among the data in the 4 datasets? After all, they all
   have the same mean, sd, and cor(x, y).





    SOURCE PAGE 10 / 64

  Anscombe’s quartet

   Even though the correlation coefficients are identical, data has different distributions and are
   very different when plotted.

        • Correlation does not reflect nonlinear relationships.

        • Correlation coefficient is sensitive to outliers.

  Correlation Interpretation

  Remember: correlation measures only the degree of linear relationships!

   Correlation reflects noisiness and direction of a linear relationship.

   Correlation does not reflect the slope of a linear relationship.

   Correlation does not reflect nonlinear relationships.

    SOURCE PAGE 13 / 64

  Correlation vs Causation

   Shoe sizes vs. Grades:

   Consider elementary school --------' shoe sizes and scores on a standard reading ----. They are
   correlated but saying that larger shoe size causes higher reading scores is as absurd.

   Ice cream sales vs Shark attacks:

   Ice cream sales correlate with shark attacks. So are some types of crime rates in certain areas.
   But you cannot reduce shark attacks or crime by reducing the consumption of ice cream.

   Confounding/Lurking/Common Response Variable

  A typical reason for why variables are correlated but do not have a causal relationship is a
   confounding variable that creates a spurious (false) correlation.

   Confound variable is an external variable / factor that influences both X and Y variables thus
   making it seem like there is a statistical relationship between X and Y, but it is caused by a
   third variable.

   e.g. older -------- had more practice with ----- and -------- thus do better e.g. due to it being the
  summer time more swimmers are in the water

  London Cholera Outbreaks in the 1850s

  miasma or ‘bad air’: Bad smells given off by waste and rotting matter and believed to be the
   main source of cholera

   Source: John Leech's cartoon in Punch, 23 (25 September 1852): 139 http://www.victorian‐
   web.org/science/health/cholera/cholera.html





    SOURCE PAGE 15 / 64

  John Snow

   John Snow is regarded as one of the founding fathers of modern epidemiology who believed
   that cholera spread through contaminated water. This contradicted the prevailing theory that
   diseases were spread by miasma in the air.

   The September 1854 cholera outbreak was centered in the Soho district, close to Snow's
   house. Snow mapped the 13 public wells and all the known cholera deaths around Soho, and
   noted the spatial clustering of cases around one particular water pump on the southwest
   corner of the intersection of Broad (now Broadwick) Street and Cambridge (now Lexington)
   Street.

  He examined water samples from various wells under a microscope, and confirmed the pres‐
   ence of an unknown bacterium in the Broad Street samples. Despite strong scepticism from
   the local authorities, he had the pump handle removed from the Broad Street pump and the
   outbreak quickly subsided.

   can be ascribed to the treatment.

  Modeling

   Analyzing Individual Variables So far, we have analyzed individual variables by forming
   confidence intervals and hypothesis -------.

   Analyzing Relationships Between Variables Next, we will analyze relationships between one or
  more variables. Our goal is to build models with explanatory power to predict performance.

   Applications:

        • Understanding factors that drive financial index/ ETF performance

        • Forecast investment return or business sales

  Why Analyze Relationships?

   In Finance we want to know how are stock prices affected by market movements?

  What is the impact of mergers on stockholder’s value?

   In Marketing, how affective are different type of advertising?

  Do promotions simply shift sales without affecting the overall volume?

   In Economics how do interest rates affect consumer behavior?

  How do trade policies influence imports/exports?

    SOURCE PAGE 25 / 64

  Two Purposes of Regression

   Statistics / Econometrics: you should have theoretical reason to include each variable in your
   equation.

   Machine Learning: automatic selection of the best independent variables from the ones
   provided.

   Prediction Explanation Focus on Y Focus on x Predict the future Explain effect of x on Y

   You try to make the best prediction of Y e.g. Predicting the price of a used Prius e.g. Netflix
   trying to guess your next show

   You try to explain the effect that specific variables, x′s, have on Y e.g. Looking at the effect of
   mileage on the price of a used Prius e.g. Netflix looking at the effect of time of day on show
   selection

  Estimates of Residual Errors

  We want to make the residuals:

  We can visualize residuals using a Residual Error Plot.

          1. Have an average of zero (this is equivalent to saying ‘there is no bias’)

          2. Be “as small as possible” (by minimizing the squares of the errors with respect to
          coefficients). This is equivalent to saying “we want to minimize the standard deviation of
        the residual errors”.

  Significance of Coefficients

  We have found the coefficients of the equation:

   ෢ criminalsi= መβ0 + መβ1 ∗pubsi

   Rule is:

        • Always keep the intercept in the equation as it allows the regression line to not be
         fixed at the origin

        • Decide if coefficient of the x variable is significantly different from 0.

   Q: Why do we need to decide that?





    SOURCE PAGE 38 / 64

  Significance of Coefficients

  We have found the coefficients of the equation:

   ෢ criminalsi= መβ0 + መβ1 ∗pubsi

     If መβ1 = 0, then pubs has no influence on criminals since the equation becomes: ෢ criminalsi=
   መβ0.

   Let’s establish whether the public_houses variable has predictive power on the crime variable
   at α= 5%.

   Hypothesis ------- for Regression Coefficients H0: መβ1 = 0 implies no relationship between x
   and Y H1: መβ1 ≠0 coefficient is significant

        • Since the public_houses p-value 0.0026 < 0.05 we can reject H0 and conclude the
          coefficient is significant.

        • Alternatively, you can base your decision on the t-stat, since |3.22| > 2, reject the null
         hypothesis.

   variable xt is zero.

   The coefficient: change in the expected value of yt corresponding to 1 unit increase in xt.

   the dependent variable and the regression equation reduces down to ෢ criminalsi= መβ0

   The variable xt has a relationship with the variable we are trying to predict.

  ෢β1−0

    t-stat =

   S෢β1

  We only need the t-stat of መβ1 since we always keep the intercept regardless if it is significant
   or not. The tstat of መβ1 is 0.2814−0

   0.6505 = 0.433

    SOURCE PAGE 41 / 64

  Point Prediction and Prediction Interval

   Valid Model: all coefficients are significant (except the intercept which we always keep).

  Once we ensure the model is valid, we can write down the equation of the fitted regression
    line as:

   ෢ criminalsi= 109.34 + 0.1162 ∗pubsi

   This equation can be used to make a point prediction. A single-valued estimate of ෢Yt for a
   given value of xt is obtained by inserting the value of xt:

   ෢ criminalsi= 109.34 + 0.1162 ∗72 = 117.98

   However, how certain are we about this value?

   Prediction Interval Use the residual standard error to form approximate prediction interval for
   ෢Yt for the given value of xt.

   ෢Yt± 1.96 ∗S

   Example: for xt= 72, ෢Yt= 117.98, the interval is:

   117.98 1.96 ∗37.2 = [45.07, 190.89]

    SOURCE PAGE 43 / 64

  Residual Standard Error

   Residual Standard Error (RSE) is the square root of the average squared residuals:

   n yi−ොyi2

  RSE= se= σi=1

  n−p−1

   where n is the number of observations and p number of independent variables.

   Importance of RSE:

   Measure of Model Accuracy: how well model predicts the observed data (smaller se means
   better line fit).




SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  264

PAGE 265
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 4


   Comparison: compare the fit of different models by selecting the one with the smaller se

   Model Adequacy: compare RSE to standard deviation of the dependent variable (if se ≫σY
   then model is not capturing the data patterns well).





    SOURCE PAGE 44 / 64

  R2

   Coefficient of Determination, R2 = corr2 describes ‘goodness of fit’ of a regression model i.e.
  how well does the line fit the data?

        • Model is never perfect

        • Model captures part of the variability of the data

  R2 = 1 line fits the data perfectly R2 = 0 model explains none of the variability in Y

     It is calculated as:

   σ ෢Yi−തY

  R2 = Explained Variation

   σ Yi−തY2 = corr2

   Total Variation =

  2 is the variance of the fitted ෢Yi points and σ Yi−തY2 is the variance of the original Y points

   where σ ෢Yi−തY

   Interpretation of R2

        • R2 shows how much better your model is compared to the unconditional forecast
         (naïve model) that predicts every value of Y to be the mean(Y)?

   n yi n−1

   ෢Yt= തY= σi=1

        • R2 shows the proportion of total variation of Y that is explained by the model (i.e. by
        the independent variable(s))





    SOURCE PAGE 45 / 64

  R2

   The higher the R2 the greater the explanatory power of the model.

    SOURCE PAGE 46 / 64

  Adjusted R2

   Adjusted R2

   Adjusts the R2 statistic for the number of independent variables present in the model.

        • As the number of inputs (x’s) increases, R2 typically increases regardless of whether
        the variables are useful for prediction.

        • Adjusted R2 will only increase if the new x variable improves the model more than
        would be expected by chance.

  = 1 −(n−1)

  n−p−1 1 −R2

   Radj

   where n is the number of observations and p number of independent variables. If n is very
   large and p is very small, the ratio is close to zero, and R2 ≈Radj

   Negative Adj R2:

   which means that the model fits worse than the naïve model.

     It is possible to have negative values of Radj

     It can happen because:

        • No intercept was used (forcing the line to go through origin doesn’t make sense for
       many real-life tasks)

        • Overfitting (great performance on training data with

   but poor out-of-sample prediction with

   high Radj

    )

   low/negative Radj

   Model Selection:

  When selecting among competing models, select the one where all variables are significant,
   the model has the largest Adj R2, and smallest RSE.

    SOURCE PAGE 53 / 64

  Linear Regression Model Assumptions

   Assumptions:

   [A1] Relationship between x and Y is linear.

   [A2] Randomness in Y values comes purely from the error term ε. Values of the independent
   variable x are assumed fixed and not random.

   [A3] Errors are uncorrelated with independent variables, x.

   [A4] Errors are uncorrelated with each other in successive observations i.e. errors are
   independent of each other.

   Assumptions:

   [A5] Errors are Normally distributed with mean 0 and variance σ2, ε~N(0, σ2). Note: constant,
   time independent variance is called homoscedasticity.

   ε~N(0, σ2) assumption is essential for:

        • Hypothesis ------- of regression coefficients.

        • Interval estimation around point prediction.

        • Model validity: “are residuals Normally distributed?” ➢Normal residuals: model cor‐
          rectly specified ➢Nonnormal residuals: nonlinearity present, interactions between
        independent variables, outliers





    SOURCE PAGE 54 / 64

  How Residuals Should Look

  Random scatter with no visible pattern.

   Constant variance of the residuals

    SOURCE PAGE 55 / 64

  Regression Error Analysis

  We should not be making systematic errors.

   Systematic error: means errors exhibit some consistent, non-random pattern, rather than
   being distributed randomly around the regression line.

   Systematic error presence means regression model is not fully capturing the relationship
   between Y and x’s.

  Any systematic component should be in the model rather than in the error.

  By including the systematic error in the model, the model should improve.

   outcomei= modeli+ errori

    yi

    xi Systematic part

    εi Unsystematic part

   Possible Reasons For Systematic Errors:

        • Nonlinearity: systematic pattern in the residuals

        • Heteroscedasticity: variance of errors changes across levels of independent variable

        • Autocorrelation: errors in one period are correlated

   with errors in another period





    SOURCE PAGE 56 / 64

  Systematic Errors: Nonlinear Relationship

   True underlying relationship is nonlinear, however a line was fitted

  A systematic patter can by seen due to errors above and below the fitted line

   Remedy: nonlinear transformation (next session)





    SOURCE PAGE 57 / 64

  Systematic Errors: Heteroscedasticity

   Variance of residuals is not constant.

   Non-consistent standard deviation of the variable over time.

   Remedy: standard error clustering

    SOURCE PAGE 58 / 64

  Systematic Errors: Autocorrelation

   Serial correlation / autocorrelation: means errors are correlated with each other over time. It
   violates the assumption of independence of errors.

   The residual plot shows a clear linear pattern.

   You may also see a wave-like or cyclical pattern.

   Remedy: introduce lags.

   Example:

   ෢ Salest= ොa+ ෢bAdvertisingt+ ƸcAdvertisingt−1

  Examine residuals using Autoplot

     If something goes wrong in our model, it will show up in the residuals. Therefore, always plot
   the residuals.

   Use the ggfortify library to plot 3 essential plots for residuals.


      library(ggfortify) model1 %>% autoplot(which = 1:3) + theme_bw()


   The Three Plots Show:

          1. Residuals vs Fitted Values (i.e. ε vs ෢Y, the plot on pp. 51).

  Want to see: a horizontal straight line.

          2. Normal Q-Q Plot (i.e. quantile quantile plot of theoretical normal distribution vs the
         quantiles of the residuals) Want to see: a 45-degree line.

          3. Spread-Location (i.e. sqrt of absolute values of standardized residuals) Want to see: a
         horizontal straight line.

Estiamtes of Residual Errors

We can visualize residuals on a Residual Error Plot. It is nothing else but the errors themselves,
plotted using the regression line plot, which has been turned around to make it visually more ac‐
cessible.


   # ---------- Model 1 (Simple Linear Regression) -----------
   model1 <- lm(criminals ~ public_houses, data = crime) # single x

   crime$predicted <- predict(model1)  # Y_hat values that will sit on the regression line
   crime$residuals <- residuals(model1) # error between Ys and Y_hats

   # Plot 1
   ggplot(crime, aes(x = public_houses, y = criminals)) +
     geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "blue") +
     geom_segment(aes(xend = public_houses, yend = predicted), colour = "red") +
     geom_point() +
     geom_point(aes(y = predicted), shape = 1) +
     labs(title = "Relationship between Crime and Pubs, England 1856",
     x = "Pubs per 100K population",
     y = "Criminals per 100K population")

   # Plot 2
   crime$predicted_zero <- c(0)
   ggplot(crime, aes(x = public_houses, y = residuals)) +
     geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "blue") +
     geom_point(aes(y = predicted_zero), shape = 1) +
     geom_segment(aes(xend = public_houses, yend = predicted_zero), colour = "red") +
     geom_point() +
     labs(title = "Relationship between Crime and Pubs, England 1856",
     x = "Pubs per 100K population",
     y = "Distance from line")

What drives used Prius prices?

A recent article in the UK claimed that [your Uber cab is most likely to be a Toyota Prius](https://
www.motoringresearch.com/car-news/your-uber-cab-is-most-likely-to-be-a-toyota-prius-and-why-
thats-a-good-thing/).

Let's carry out analyses of the relationships between price and mileage.

Loading the data set, summary statistics


   prius <- read_csv("toyota_prius_jun18.csv")
   glimpse(prius)


The prius tibble contains prices of used Toyota Prius in the UK that were gathered in June 2018.
`town`, `region` and `colour` are categorical variables (character data type <chr>), whereas
`miles` and `price` are numerical variables (numeric data type <dbl>). `year` and `engine` are
treated as numerical variables, but in reality are categorical variables.

Turn 'engine' into categorical variable (factor), and create a new column for the car age:


   prius <- prius %>%
     mutate(engine = factor(engine), # turn it to a factor
     car_age = 2018 - year)

   favstats(price ~ year,  data=prius)
   favstats(price ~ engine, data=prius)
   favstats(price ~ colour, data=prius)


First we will obtain the scatter plot to see the potential relationship between price and miles.
Then we will add the line of the best fit (visually this is the regression line, but you will create the
actual regression model yourself below).


   # plot scatter plot
   ggplot(prius, aes(x = miles, y = price)) +
     geom_point() +
     theme_bw()

   # examine correlation between
   prius %>%
     dplyr::select(price, miles) %>%
     ggpairs()



   # plot scatter plot and add the best straight line
   ggplot(prius, aes(x = miles, y = price)) +
     geom_point() +
     theme_bw() +
     geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)


Simple Regression: Relationship between price and miles


   # run linear regression to create a variable called car_model1, using lm() model
   car_model1 <- lm(price ~ miles, data = prius)

   Multiple Linear Regression: generalize simple linear regression to deal with a set of
   independent variables that helps to predict Y.

        • build more powerful model by taking other relevant

   inputs into account

        • produce better forecasts with smaller confidence

        hypothesis -------)

  መβmxm,t

  m independent variables used to build the model x1,t,…, xm,t

   The slope βi provides the value for the change in Yt per unit increase in xi,t while other
   independent variables are kept fixed

   The intercept β0 is a “baseline” scenario: what happens to Yt in the case where xt is

    SOURCE PAGE 30 / 56

  Interaction Terms

   Interaction Term an independent variable in a regression model that is a product of two
   independent variables.

   Sometimes the partial effect of the dependent variable with respect to independent variable
   can depend on magnitude of yet another independent variable.

   Forming An Interaction Term

   Does the effect x1 on Y depend on the level of x2?




SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  292

PAGE 293
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 5


  Y= β0 + β1x1 + β2x2 + β3x1 ∗x2 + e

   Example:

   Does a drug have more effect on women (0) than men (1) in cholesterol prediction?

   Cℎolesterol = β0 + β1drug+ β2gender+ β3drug∗gender+ e

     If መβ3 < 0 and significant, it means that the drug lowers cholesterol by more units in men
   than in women.

   Hierarchy Principle:

     If you include the interaction term β3x1 ∗x2, you should also include the main effects of the
   involved variables, i.e. include β1x1 and β2x2 in the fitted equation as well, even if they are
   not significant. This ensures the model is hierarchically well-specified.





    SOURCE PAGE 31 / 56

  Interaction Terms: Example Prius Car Price

   Example: Prius Car Price

   Qn: “Does car price drop more for a particular engine for milage?

   price = β0 + β1miles+ β2engine+ β3miles∗engine+ e

   Interaction term lets us examine whether:

        • The effect of miles on price, depends not only on the miles itself, but also on the type
         of engine the car has.

        • The mileage impact on price might be different for a small-engine car versus a large-
        engine car.

        • If መβ3 < 0 this means, there is a negative impact on car price when both high milage
       and large engine size are present.

    SOURCE PAGE 33 / 56

   Multicollinearity

   Multicollinearity appears when independent variables used inside the regression equation are
   highly correlated.

   Effects:

        • Not much added predictive power.

        • Additional variables add little information.

        • Magnitude/signs of regression coefficients are different from expected.

        • May cause two or more variables to become insignificant but significance may be high
               if one variable is dropped.

        • Parameter estimates are unreliable.

   Remedial Action:

        • Remove one of the correlated variables.

        • Check for correlations between independent variables in advance of running the re‐
         gression

    ---- in RStudio:

   Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) assess multicollinearity in regression models, providing a value
   for each independent variable.


      library(car) car::vif(model)


    - VIF > 10: high multicollinearity, attend to it - VIF 5 -10: moderate multicollinearity, keep an
   eye - VIF < 5: no multicollinearity, acceptable





    SOURCE PAGE 34 / 56

  Distributed Lag Model

   Distributed lag model is a model for time series data in which a regression equation is used to
   predict current values of a dependent variable based on both the current values of an
   independent variable and/or its lagged (past period) values.


      True (Assumed) Model:


   Yt= β0 + β1xt+ β2xt−1 + β3xt−2 + ⋯+ εt

  Assume a finite number of lags (e.g. 2-5) and run the multiple regression model as usual.

  Remove insignificant lags one by one starting with least significant first and re-run the model.

   Data Preparation:

    t Yt xt

    t Yt xt xt−1

  NA

   13.3 3.4

   10.2 5.1

   10.2 5.1 3.4

   1.3

   1.3 5.1

   After creating the required columns, remove any rows with NA.

   To create lags with dplyr, read here.

  Event -----

   Event ----- is a model applied when you are interested in the dynamic treatment effect, i.e.,
  how does an outcome change several periods before and after an event?

   Analysis setup: two (groups of) observations i are both observed for multiple periods before
   and after time t, when group A is treated (experienced an event), while group B is not treated.


      True (Assumed) Model:


   Yit= β0 + βt−2Ιt−2Ti+ βtΙtTi+ βt+1Ιt+1Ti… + εit

   The t-1 period is omitted as the reference period.

   Data Preparation:

   Create extra columns for each lead and lag, as (suppose the event took place at time period
   3):

      i t Yt Ti

      i t Yt Ti Ιt−2 Ιt Ιt+1

  Regression with Dummy Variable: War

  Dummy variable can be used in regression analysis just like any other quantitative variable.
  We have 2 categories: war / no war and a single dummy variable to represent it.

   Fitted Model:

   ෢ bond= መβ0 + መβ1GNP+ መβ2WAR = 1.02 + 0.72 ∗GNP+ 2 ∗War

   Interpretation:

   Intercept is the bond price for the reference group

   Positive β2 coefficient (+2.0 in this case) means that bond price was higher for the dummy
   variable (war) than the reference group (no war).

   Negative β2 coefficient would have meant that bond price would have been lower.

  Regression with k-levels

  When a categorical variable has k categories (we call them ‘levels), we include only k-1
  dummy variables in the regression model.

   The category that is left out is usually the one with the most frequent observations and it acts
   as a reference.

   Example:

        • 3 movie categories: adventure, romance, drama.

        • If drama has the most obs, leave it out as a reference and create 2 dummies for
        adventure and romance.

   salest= β0 + β1promot+ β2adventuret+ β3romancet+ εt

  Dummies

   k-th category is redundant information:

  Obs promo adventure romance drama

   12.5

   10.2

   14.5

  … … … … …

   Obs1: if its not adventure or romance then those 2 pieces of information tell us it must be
   drama.

   Obs2: if it is not adventure but it is romance, then automatically we know it is not drama, etc.





SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  300

PAGE 301
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 5

    SOURCE PAGE 52 / 56

  Regression Check List

   Set up the model, choose the data - Which variables to include - Generate dummy variables
   where appropriate - What do expect (from practice, theory,

   anecdotal evidence)?

   Check scatter plots and correlations - Identify any obvious nonlinearities (transform variables)
    - Beware of high correlations between explanatory factors (multicollinearility)

   Carry out the regression - Drop insignificant variables (one-by-one starting with least signific‐
   ant first) and re-model - Ensure the model is valid (i.e. all coefficients are significant; always
   keep the intercept) - Check residual plots with autoplot() function

   Choose the best model - Compare models with huxreg() function - Highest Adjusted R2, and
   lowest standard error of

   residuals - Compare to initial expectations

   Use the model to create forecasts

  Interaction Terms

   Interaction Term an independent variable in a regression model that is a product of two
   independent variables.

   Sometimes the partial effect of the dependent variable with respect to independent variable
   can depend on magnitude of yet another independent variable.

   Forming An Interaction Term

   Does the effect x1 on Y depend on the level of x2?

  Y= β0 + β1x1 + β2x2 + β3x1 ∗x2 + e

   Example:

   Does a drug have more effect on women (0) than men (1) in cholesterol prediction?

   Cℎolesterol = β0 + β1drug+ β2gender+ β3drug∗gender+ e

     If መβ3 < 0 and significant, it means that the drug lowers cholesterol by more units in men
   than in women.

   Hierarchy Principle:

     If you include the interaction term β3x1 ∗x2, you should also include the main effects of the
   involved variables, i.e. include β1x1 and β2x2 in the fitted equation as well, even if they are
   not significant. This ensures the model is hierarchically well-specified.

  Interaction Terms: Example Prius Car Price

   Example: Prius Car Price

   Qn: “Does car price drop more for a particular engine for milage?

   price = β0 + β1miles+ β2engine+ β3miles∗engine+ e

   Interaction term lets us examine whether:

        • The effect of miles on price, depends not only on the miles itself, but also on the type
         of engine the car has.

        • The mileage impact on price might be different for a small-engine car versus a large-
        engine car.

        • If መβ3 < 0 this means, there is a negative impact on car price when both high milage
       and large engine size are present.

    SOURCE PAGE 35 / 60

   Multicollinearity

   Multicollinearity appears when independent variables used inside the regression equation are
   highly correlated.

   Effects:

        • Not much added predictive power.

        • Additional variables add little information.

        • Magnitude/signs of regression coefficients are different from expected.

        • May cause two or more variables to become insignificant but significance may be high
               if one variable is dropped.

        • Parameter estimates are unreliable.

   Remedial Action:

        • Remove one of the correlated variables.

        • Check for correlations between independent variables in advance of running the re‐
         gression

    ---- in RStudio:

   Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) assess multicollinearity in regression models, providing a value
   for each independent variable.


      library(car) car::vif(model)


    - VIF > 10: high multicollinearity, attend to it - VIF 5 -10: moderate multicollinearity, keep an
   eye - VIF < 5: no multicollinearity, acceptable





    SOURCE PAGE 36 / 60

  Distributed Lag Model

   Distributed lag model is a model for time series data in which a regression equation is used to
   predict current values of a dependent variable based on both the current values of an
   independent variable and/or its lagged (past period) values.


      True (Assumed) Model:


   Yt= β0 + β1xt+ β2xt−1 + β3xt−2 + ⋯+ εt

  Assume a finite number of lags (e.g. 2-5) and run the multiple regression model as usual.

  Remove insignificant lags one by one starting with least significant first and re-run the model.

   Data Preparation:

  Event -----

   Event ----- is a model applied when you are interested in the dynamic treatment effect, i.e.,
  how does an outcome change several periods before and after an event?

   Analysis setup: two (groups of) observations i are both observed for multiple periods before
   and after time t, when group A is treated (Ti=1), while group B is not treated (Ti=0).


      True (Assumed) Model:


   Yit= β0 + βt−2Ιt−2Ti+ βtΙtTi+ βt+1Ιt+1Ti… + εit

   The t-1 period is omitted as the reference period.

   Data Preparation:

   Create extra columns for each lead and lag, as (suppose the event took place at time period 3
   and the event happened to unit 2 but not unit 1):

      i t Yt Ti

      i t Yt Ti Ιt−2 Ιt Ιt+1

  Dummy variable can be used in regression analysis just like any other quantitative variable.
  We have 2 categories: war / no war and a single dummy variable to represent it.

   Interpretation:

   Positive β2 coefficient (+2.0 in this case) means that bond price was higher for the dummy
   variable (war) than the reference group (no war).

   Negative β2 coefficient would have meant that bond price would have been lower.

  Regression with k-levels

  When a categorical variable has k categories (we call them ‘levels), we include only k-1
  dummy variables in the regression model.

   The category that is left out is usually the one with the most frequent observations and it acts
   as a reference.

   Example:

        • 3 movie categories: adventure, romance, drama.

        • If drama has the most obs, leave it out as a reference and create 2 dummies for
        adventure and romance.

   salest= β0 + β1promot+ β2adventuret+ β3romancet+ εt

  Dummies

   k-th category is redundant information:

  Obs promo adventure romance drama

   12.5

   10.2

   14.5

  … … … … …

   Obs1: if its not adventure or romance then those 2 pieces of information tell us it must be
   drama.

   Obs2: if it is not adventure but it is romance, then automatically we know it is not drama, etc.

     If ෢ β2 > 0 then ticket sales were higher for the dummy variable adventure, than the reference
   group drama.

   adventure=0 romance=1

   sales

   adventure=1 romance=0

   ෢ β0 + ෢ β3

   adventure=0 romance=0

   ෢ β0 + ෢ β2

   ෢ β0

   Promotion

    SOURCE PAGE 54 / 60

  Regression Check List

   Set up the model, choose the data - Which variables to include - Generate dummy variables
   where appropriate - What do expect (from practice, theory,

   anecdotal evidence)?

   Check scatter plots and correlations - Identify any obvious nonlinearities (transform variables)
    - Beware of high correlations between explanatory factors (multicollinearility)

   Carry out the regression - Drop insignificant variables (one-by-one starting with least signific‐
   ant first) and re-model - Ensure the model is valid (i.e. all coefficients are significant; always
   keep the intercept) - Check residual plots with autoplot() function

   Choose the best model - Compare models with huxreg() function - Highest Adjusted R2, and
   lowest standard error of

   residuals - Compare to initial expectations

   Use the model to create forecasts

Include Interaction Term:

This means that the effect of mileage depends on engine size. If we have two explanatory vari‐
ables, and the value of one (effect of mileage) depends on the other (engine size), then besides
the two variables, we also introduce an interaction variable, which is the product of the two.


   # Model 3: Xs: miles, engine, car_age, miles*engine
   prius_transformed1
   <-
   prius

Mutlicollinearity

The code library(car) and car::vif(model1) is used in R to assess multicollinearity in regression
models by calculating the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) for each predictor variable in the model.

Interpret the VIF values:

      VIF > 10: Indicates high multicollinearity, which could make your model unstable.

      VIF between 5 and 10: Moderate multicollinearity, something to keep an eye on.

      VIF < 5: Low or no multicollinearity, typically acceptable.


   model2
   <-
   lm
   (criminals

EXPLANATION Model 1 assumes a common slope, while Model 2/3 do not assume that. Implicitly
Model 1 assumes the error term has the same distribution for both d=0 and d=1, while Model 2/3
do not assume that. The implicit or explicit assumptions on the error distributions affect the finite-
sample distribution of the estimators of intercepts and slopes.

Winner Case -----

At the last board meeting of Winner Plc., the headquarters of a large multinational company, the
issue was raised that women were being discriminated in the company, in the sense that the
salaries were not the same for male and female executives. A quick analysis of a sample of 50
employees (of which 24 men and 26 women) revealed that the average salary for men was about
8,400 higher than for women. This seemed like a considerable difference, so it was decided that a
further analysis of the company salaries was warranted.

The objective is to find out whether there is indeed a significant difference between the salaries
of men and women, and whether the difference is due to discrimination or whether it is based on
another determining factor.

Nonlinear Transformations

I provide 3 toy datasets of x and y variables.

Data 1


   set.seed(123)
   x <- c(1:10)
   y <- 5 + 3*x^2 + rnorm(10, mean = 2, sd = 5)

   data1 <- tibble(x, y) %>%
     dplyr::select(y, x)
   # Sometimes multiple R packages have functions with the same name. Use "dplyr::" to specify
   the package that the function "select" belongs to.

   # visualize the data and the fitted regression line
   ggplot(data1, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
     geom_point() +
     geom_line() +
     geom_smooth(method='lm', se=FALSE) +
     labs(x="x", y="y")

   # create an initial regression model between y and x
   model1_data1 <- lm(y ~ x)
   summary(model1_data1)


We can see that the first dataset looks like an x^2 relationship. Therefore perform the transform‐
ation and create a new variable, $z=x^2$ and re-run the linear regression:


   data1_transformed <- data1 %>%
     dplyr::mutate(z = x^2) %>%
     dplyr::select(y, z)

   model2_data1 <- lm(y ~ z, data=data1_transformed)



SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  367

PAGE 368
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                     Lecture 5


   summary(model2_data1)

   ggplot(data1_transformed, aes(x=z, y=y)) +
     geom_point() +
     geom_line() +
     geom_smooth(method='lm', se=FALSE) +
     labs(x="x^2", y="y")


We can see that the transformation improved the regression model fit (using R2) from 0.957 to
0.998.

Data 2


   set.seed(123)
   x <- c(1:10)

     round(2)

     geom_point() +

     geom_smooth(method='lm', se=FALSE) +
     labs(x="x", y="y")

   # create an initial regression model between y and x
   model1_data2 <- lm(y ~ x)
   summary(model1_data2)


We can see that the second dataset looks like an 1/x relationship. Therefore perform the trans‐
formation and create a new variable, $z=1/x$ and re-run the linear regression:


   data2_transformed <- data2 %>%
     dplyr::mutate(z = 1/x) %>%
     dplyr::select(y, z)

   model2_data2 <- lm(y ~ z, data=data2_transformed)

We can see that the transformation improved the regression model fit (using R2) from 0.734 to
0.971.
