Reduction in Impurity

Pure Group

Maximum Impurity

A group is pure if everyone in it has the same outcome (all Yes or all No). It’s impure if it’s a mix.

Our Root Node

The Intuition

If a split produces one group that’s all Yes and another that’s all No, we can predict perfectly. The
goal at every step is to get closer to that ideal.

CART

The algorithm picks the split that creates the purest child groups, and thereby produces the
biggest drop in impurity.

Gini Impurity

G0 is the impurity at the parent node before we split.

G(L) and G(R) are the impurities of the two child nodes after the split.

What matters is the drop.

Interpretation

A split is useful when the child nodes are less mixed than the parent node.

The bigger the reduction, the more that split improves purity, so CART prefers it.

Gini Impurity Formula

In our case: Gini = 1 − p Y ² − p N ²

Interpretation

0 = perfectly pure

0.5 = maximum impurity for two classes

Intuition

Draw two members of this node independently with replacement. Gini impurity is the probability
that their outcomes differ.

Root Node Calculation

Our 12 subscribers: 8 Yes , 4 No

This is our starting impurity . Close to the maximum of 0.5 because our data has a genuine mix of
outcomes.

Training and ---- Accuracy


 Prediction rule                     Training Accuracy                         ---- Accuracy

 Depth 1                      75% (9/12)                    50% (3/6)

 Depth 2                      92% (11/12)                   67% (4/6)

 Depth 3                       100% (12/12)                  50% (3/6)

 Always predict renewal            67% (8/12)                    83% (5/6)


The always-renew rule gets the most ---- cases right. Among the trees, adding the region split at
depth 3 fixes one training error and introduces one ---- error.

Lesson

Perfect training accuracy does not mean good predictions on new data. Always ---- on held-out
data.

Overfitting

As the tree grows deeper:

Training accuracy keeps increasing (the tree memorizes more)

---- accuracy first increases, then decreases (overfitting begins)

The optimal depth is where the ---- accuracy is maximized.

Ways to overcome Overfitting

To avoid overfitting the training data, you need to restrict the Decision Tree's freedom during
training, also known as regularization .

1. Pre-pruning

Key hyperparameters: Maximum depth, minimum samples to split, minimum samples per leaf,
maximum leaf nodes and maximum features.

Increasing the min* hyperparameters and reducing the max* hyperparameters will regularize the
model.




SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  708

PAGE 709
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                   Lecture 10


2. Post-pruning

Grow the full tree first, then remove the branches that add more complexity than they do accur‐
acy.

err ( T ) is the fraction of training records that are misclassified; L ( T ) is the number of leaf nodes
(terminal nodes); and α is the penalty ("complexity parameter") for tree size.


 Prediction rule                     Training Accuracy                         ---- Accuracy

 Depth 1                      75% (9/12)                    50% (3/6)

 Depth 2                      92% (11/12)                   67% (4/6)

 Depth 3                       100% (12/12)                  50% (3/6)

 Always predict renewal            67% (8/12)                    83% (5/6)


Which rule would you use to decide whom to contact: the always-renew rule with 83% ---- set
accuracy or the depth-two tree with 67% accuracy?

Confusion Matrices

Same six ---- subscribers. Leaving is the positive outcome (Renew = No).


 Actual outcome                   Predicted leave                   Predicted renew

  Left                             1 True positive                    0 False negatives

 Renewed                         2 False positives                   3 True negatives



 Actual outcome                   Predicted leave                   Predicted renew

  Left                             0 True positives                    1 False negative

 Renewed                         0 False positives                   5 True negatives


Predicting renewal for everyone misses the only churner. Depth 2 is preferable here if missing
that churner costs more than following up with two subscribers who renewed.

Continuous Features

Continuous Feature: Viewing Hours

Suppose we observe weekly viewing hours instead of classifying subscribers as Binge or Casual.


 Subscriber                      Viewing hours                 Renew?

 A                                                           No

 B                                                           No

 C                                                           No

 D                                                                          Yes

 E                                                           No

 F                                                                          Yes

 G                                                                          Yes


Where could CART split?

CART first sorts the observed values:

It then ----- the midpoint of every gap:





SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  710

PAGE 711
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                   Lecture 10


Choosing the Split Point

For every threshold t , CART compares subscribers with viewing hours ≤ t against those with
viewing hours > t .


 Threshold                 Left child                Right child              Weighted Gini

 1.5                     0 Yes, 1 No               3 Yes, 3 No                 0.429

 2.5                     0 Yes, 2 No               3 Yes, 2 No                 0.343

 4.0                     0 Yes, 3 No               3 Yes, 1 No                 0.214

 6.0                     1 Yes, 3 No               2 Yes, 1 No                 0.405

 7.5                     1 Yes, 4 No               2 Yes, 0 No                 0.229

 9.0                     2 Yes, 4 No               1 Yes, 0 No                 0.381


Lowest weighted Gini: split at viewing hours ≤ 4.

Efficient Gini Calculation

CART scans the sorted observations once. In this example, each step moves one observation from
the right child to the left child and updates the class counts.


 Scan position              Left child                Right child              Weighted Gini

  Start                    0 Yes, 0 No               3 Yes, 4 No          —

  After 1 hour               0 Yes, 1 No               3 Yes, 3 No                 0.429

  After 2 hours              0 Yes, 2 No               3 Yes, 2 No                 0.343

  After 3 hours              0 Yes, 3 No               3 Yes, 1 No                 0.214


CART updates the class counts rather than rereading every observation in each child node.

Entropy

Entropy & Information Gain

Entropy Formula

For two classes, H = −p Y log 2 p Y − p N log 2 p N .

Entropy ranges from 0 bits for a pure node to 1 bit for an even split between the two classes.

Root Node Calculation

8 Yes, 4 No (p Y = 2/3, p N = 1/3)

Entropy Reduction for Each Feature

Information Gain = entropy before the split − weighted entropy after the split. Each child is
weighted by its share of subscribers. Gains are rounded at the end.





SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  711

PAGE 712
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                   Lecture 10


Viewing Pattern

Binge (5): H = 0

Casual (7): H ≈ 0.985

Information Gain ≈ 0.344 bits

Plan Type

Basic (8): H = 1

Premium (4): H = 0

Information Gain ≈ 0.252 bits

Region

Urban (9): H ≈ 0.991

Rural (3): H = 0

Information Gain ≈ 0.175 bits

Gini vs. Entropy: Same Answer


 Measure                Viewing Pattern          Plan Type               Region

  Gini Gain                   0.159                      0.111                      0.074

 Information Gain (bits)       0.344                      0.252                      0.175

 Winner              ✓                 ✗                 ✗


Both measures rank these three splits in the same order. Gini is faster (no logarithms). Entropy is
more theoretically grounded (information theory).

It is sometimes useful to group data into different time periods to ----- historical data. For ex‐
ample, we often refer to decades such as 1970s, 1980s, 1990s etc. to refer to a period of time.
(Reminder: NASA calculates a temperature anomaly, as THE difference form the base period of

   comparison <- tidyweather %>%
     filter(Year>= 1881) %>% # remove years prior to 1881
     # create new variable 'interval', and assign values based on criteria below
     mutate(interval = case_when(
     Year %in% c(1881:1920) ~ "1881-1920",
     Year %in% c(1921:1950) ~ "1921-1950",
     Year %in% c(1951:1980) ~ "1951-1980",
     Year %in% c(1981:2010) ~ "1981-2010",
     TRUE ~ "2011-present"))

Task 3: Plane Crashes

Let us look at some data about airplane crashes (from [Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/sauro‐
grandi/airplane-crashes-since-1908/)). This dataset lists all plane crashes between 1908 and
2009. Because this is real world data, it's messy, so we'll create a few extra variables and get rid
of incomplete rows. I am providing the code to clean the data in the cell below, so you don't have
to worry about it.


   library(lubridate)  # Loads functions like mdy(), year(), and month() that make handling of
   dates easy

   crashes_raw <- read_csv(here::here("Data", "Airplane_Crashes_and_Fatalities_Since_1908.csv"))

   crashes <- crashes_raw %>%
     # Create new variables related to dates
     mutate(Date = mdy(Date),
     Year = year(Date),
     Month = month(Date, label = TRUE)) %>%

     # Get rid of rows with missing data or where there were no fatalities
     filter(!is.na(Fatalities),
     !is.na(Aboard),
     !is.na(Operator),
     Fatalities > 0,) %>%

     # Make a new variable that indicates if the flight was operated by the military
     mutate(Military = ifelse(str_detect(Operator, "Military"), "Military", "Not military")) %>%

     # Make a new variable that shows what percentage of people on the flight died
     mutate(percent_passengers_died = Fatalities / Aboard)

   crashes_per_year <- crashes %>%
     count(Year)

   library(lubridate)  # Loads functions like mdy(), year(), and month() that make handling of

   crashes_raw <- read_csv("Airplane_Crashes_and_Fatalities_Since_1908.csv")

   crashes <- crashes_raw %>%
     # Create new variables related to dates
     mutate(Date = mdy(Date),
     Year = year(Date),
     Month = month(Date, label = TRUE)) %>%

     # Get rid of rows with missing data or where there were no fatalities
     filter(!is.na(Fatalities),
     !is.na(Aboard),
     !is.na(Operator),
     Fatalities > 0,) %>%

     # Make a new variable that indicates if the flight was operated by the military
     mutate(Military = ifelse(str_detect(Operator, "Military"), "Military", "Not military")) %>%

     # Make a new variable that shows what percentage of people on the flight died
     mutate(percent_passengers_died = Fatalities / Aboard)


CRASHES PER YEAR:

Summarise the data to obtain the total number of crashes for every year. Fit a curve of best fit to
the data using polynomial smoothing method.


   crashes_per_year <- crashes %>%
     group_by(Year) %>%
     summarise(count = n())

   ggplot(data = crashes_per_year, aes(x = Year, y = count)) +
     geom_point() +
     geom_line() +
     stat_smooth(method = "loess", color = "red", size = 1.5) +
     labs(x = "Year", y = "Number of crashes", title = "Polynomial fit for crashes per year")

   # --- Option 2: plot on average

     select(Year, percent_passengers_died, Military)%>%

Plane crashes were rare before 1920 and increasing thereafter (especially so throughout the
1940s). Plane crashes before 1920 are almost exclusively military. This is most likely due to the
fact that commercial air planes were not common at the time. A very large number of plane
crashes ends deadly for 100% of passengers. There are also quite a few with less than 15% dead,
however never reaching 0 (entries without fatalities were filtered earlier). In between it seems
fairly evenly scattered. However, the trendlines are both very high (80% and more) throughout,
once again highlighting that a great amount of crashes end deadly for everyone. Military plane
crashes had a fatality rate below 90% in the early 1900s, but rose to close to 100% around 1940.

Task 4: Climate change and temperature anomalies

In the last workshop, you have worked with monthly weather anomalies. However, we might be
interested in average annual anomalies. We can do this by using `group_by()` and `summar‐
ise()`, followed by a scatter plot to display the result. Find the average annual anomalies
(grouping by year) and plot these using a smoothing method.


   weather <- read_csv("https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/tabledata_v3/NH.Ts+dSST.csv",
     skip = 1,  # number of lines to skip before reading data
     na = "***") # NAs in csv are coded with ***

   tidyweather <- weather %>%
     select(Year:Dec) %>%
     pivot_longer(Jan:Dec, names_to = "Month", values_to = "delta")

   #creating yearly averages
   average_annual_anomaly <- tidyweather %>%
     group_by(Year) %>%  #grouping data by Year
     # creating summaries for mean delta
     # use `na.rm=TRUE` to eliminate NA (not available) values
     summarise(annual_average_delta = mean(delta, na.rm=TRUE))

   #plotting the data:
   ggplot(average_annual_anomaly, aes(x = Year, y = annual_average_delta)) +
     geom_point() +
     # Fit the best fit line, using LOESS method
     geom_smooth() + # note the default polynomial fit with confidence intervals around the fit.
     theme_bw() +
     labs(title = "Average Yearly Anomaly",
     y = "Average Annual Delta")

   ing that the population distribution is normal, if we built 100 such CI for different samples, 99
   of them could contain the true population mean inside the intervals.

Task 1: Confidence Intervals - Weather Anomalies

In the last workshop, you have worked with monthly weather anomalies.


   weather <- read_csv("https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/tabledata_v3/NH.Ts+dSST.csv",
     skip = 1,  # number of lines to skip before reading data
     na = "***") # NAs in csv are coded with ***

   tidyweather <- weather %>%
     select(Year:Dec) %>%
     pivot_longer(Jan:Dec, names_to = "Month", values_to = "delta")

   #creating yearly averages
   average_annual_anomaly <- tidyweather %>%
     group_by(Year) %>%  #grouping data by Year
     # creating summaries for mean delta
     # use `na.rm=TRUE` to eliminate NA (not available) values
     summarise(annual_average_delta = mean(delta, na.rm=TRUE))

   #plotting the data:
   ggplot(average_annual_anomaly, aes(x = Year, y = annual_average_delta)) +
     geom_point() +
     # Fit the best fit line, using LOESS method
     geom_smooth() + # note the default polynomial fit with confidence intervals around the fit.
     theme_bw() +
     labs(title = "Average Yearly Anomaly",
     y = "Average Annual Delta")


[NASA points out on their website](https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/world-of-change/decadal‐
temp.php) that a one-degree global change is significant because it takes a vast amount of heat
to warm all the oceans, atmosphere, and land by that much. In the past, a one- to two-degree
drop was all it took to plunge the Earth into the Little Ice Age.

We are going to work with the average temperature deviation (delta) since 2011. Construct a
**90% confidence** interval for the average annual delta since 2011. Recall that the tibble `com‐
parison` has already grouped temperature anomalies according to time intervals; we are only
interested in what is happening between 2011-present.

Hints:





SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  743

PAGE 744
COURSE ----- READER                                                                       Workshop 2


     • this tibble contains missing values, however summarise() verb expects a tibble without
     missing values. You could use na.omit() function before using summarise() in order to omit
      values that are not available.

     • obtain the number of observations before deciding if you are allowed to use the z-value or
     not (i.e. does CLT hold?)

     • if CLT holds, then proceed to calculate the confidence interval


   comparison <- tidyweather %>%
     filter(Year >= 1881) %>% # remove years prior to 1881
     # create new variable 'interval', and assign values based on criteria below
     mutate(interval =
     case_when(
     Year %in% c(1881:1920) ~ "1881-1920",
     Year %in% c(1921:1950) ~ "1921-1950",
     Year %in% c(1951:1980) ~ "1951-1980",
     Year %in% c(1981:2010) ~ "1981-2010",
     TRUE ~ "2011-present"))

   data_2011_to_present <- comparison %>%
     filter(interval == "2011-present") %>%
     na.omit() # alternatively use `na.rm=TRUE` inside each function to eliminate NA (not
   available) values

   # obtain number of delta observations
   n <- length(data_2011_to_present$delta)
   print(n)

   # since n is larger than 30 we can use the z-value by CLT
   formula_ci <- data_2011_to_present %>%
     summarise(
     mu = mean(delta),
     sigma = sd(delta),
     z_critical = qnorm(0.95), # for 90% CI we leave (100-90)/2 = 0.05% in each tail. Therefore
   we pass in 0.95
     se = sigma / sqrt(n),
     margin_of_error = z_critical*se,
     lower_ci = mu - margin_of_error,
     upper_ci = mu + margin_of_error
     )
   formula_ci


> Explain the meaning of a confidence interval. Explain the effect of using a 90% Confidence vs a
95% confidence on the width of the constructed CI.

Loosely we can say that if 100 such intervals were constructed, 95 of them would contain the true
population mean. A 90% confidence will result in a narrower CI (since we are using a smaller z-
value).

Key Definitions

Provide an explanation for each of these terms:

     • Sample Statistic : value of interest obtained from a sample, e.g. xbar.

     • Standard Error : is the standard deviation of the distribution of sample mean.

     • When should you use Standard Deviation of the sample? : in cases where sigma of
      population is not known.

     • t-Statistic : standardized difference of the sample mean from the claim expressed in
     measurement of standard error.

     • Critical level : cut-off value of the hypothesis ---- (e.g. CI; t-critical; z-critical; significance
      level)

Two separate CIs

Build two separate 95% confidence intervals for monthly mean return: one for stock INTC and
another for stock MSFT. Check if the two CIs overlap.


   stats <- myStocks_returns_monthly %>%
     filter(symbol %in% c("MSFT", "INTC")) %>%
     group_by(symbol) %>%
     summarise(xbar = mean(monthly_returns),
     sd = sd(monthly_returns),
     n = n(),
     # get t-critical value with (n-1) degrees of freedom
     t_critical = qt(0.975, n-1),
     SE = sd(monthly_returns) / sqrt(n),
     margin_of_error = t_critical * SE,
     CI_low = xbar - margin_of_error,
     CI_high = xbar + margin_of_error)

   print(stats)


INTC CI overlaps with MSFT CI, therefore we will need to carry out one of the 3 official statistical
-----, which we will learn about in the next session on hypothesis -------.

   Q5. Now, you are given a fair coin. You toss it 100 times and you get 60 heads. Using a = 0.05,
   would you come to the same conclusion that the coin is fair? (Use s = 0.5)

   z-stat (x_bar - µ )/(s/= sqrt(n) ) = 2.00

     I set a = 0.05 -> z_critical = 1.96 As the z_score > z_critical , I reject H0. The coin is not fair.

  Due to random fluctuations, you got 60 heads, assessing that the coin is not fair. However, the
   coin is actually fair.

   a represents the Type I error: the probability of rejecting H0 when H0 is actually true. Whe n
   you perform a ----, you decide the Type I error, which is the error you are willing to toller

   ate with respect to the null hypothesis.

   In this case, we’ve made a Type I error rejecting the hypothesis of fairness although the c

   oin is actually fair.

Build two separate confidence intervals for monthly mean return: one for stock INTC and another

null hypothesis ------- for differences in population mean monthly return.


   stats <- myStocks_returns_monthly %>%
     filter(symbol %in% c("MSFT", "INTC")) %>%
     group_by(symbol) %>%
     summarise(xbar = mean(monthly_returns),
     sd = sd(monthly_returns),
     n = n(),
     # get t-critical value with (n-1) degrees of freedom
     t_critical = qt(0.975, n-1),
     SE = sd(monthly_returns) / sqrt(n),
     margin_of_error = t_critical * SE,
     CI_low = xbar - margin_of_error,
     CI_high = xbar + margin_of_error)

   print(stats)

   stats <- myStocks_returns_monthly %>%
     filter(symbol %in% c("MSFT", "INTC")) %>%

     summarise(xbar = mean(monthly_returns),
     sd = sd(monthly_returns),

Joint CI

Calculate a joint CI for the mean difference in monthly returns and provide your conclusion on the
null hypothesis for stocks: INTC and MSFT. What is your conclusion about the null hypothesis?


   intc <- stats[1, ] # select 1st row with INTC information
   print(intc)

   msft <- stats[2, ] # select 2nd row with MSFT information
   print(msft)

   delta_star <- intc$xbar - msft$xbar
   z <- 2 # approx value (can also use 1.96)
   SE <- sqrt(intc$sd**2 / intc$n + msft$sd**2 / msft$n )

   # Now let's build the single confidence interval (xbar1 - xbar2) +- z*SE
   upper_CI <- delta_star + z*SE
   lower_CI <- delta_star - z*SE
   print(paste('[', round(lower_CI,3),", ", round(upper_CI,3), ']', sep=""), quote = FALSE) #
   [-0.046, 0.008]


Since 0 is included in the confidence interval, we cannot reject the null hypothesis. Therefore we
continue to hold the null hypothesis as our ground belief.

   # -------- should refer to slide 22 formula for t-stat

   t_stat <- (delta_star - 0) / (SE) # -1.4125
   print(t_stat)
   reject <- abs(t_stat) > 2 # FALSE
   print(reject)


Fail to reject the null hypothesis since absolute value of the t-stat is not greater than 2. i.e. the
sample statistic is not a surprise if null hypothesis is true.

Each row in this tibble represents a store that sells car seats. The `Sales` column measures the
number of car seats sold at that location. There are also some qualitative predictors, such as
`Shelveloc`, an indicator of the quality of the shelving location—that is, the space within a store
in which the car seat is displayed—at each location. The predictor `Shelveloc` takes on three pos‐
sible values, Bad, Medium, and Good. The predictor `Urban` takes on two possible values: Yes
and No.

Given a Simple Linear Regression setting: $Sales_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Advertising + \epsilon_i$
answer the following questions:

**Write down the null hypothesis to check if Advertising has no effect on predicting Sales.**

     • H~0~: $\beta_1 = 0$

     • H~A~: $\beta_1 \neq 0$

**---- the above hypothesis to see if Advertising can be used to predict Sales by analysing the
slope coefficient of simple linear regression between Adv and Sales.**


   model_carseats_1 <- lm(Sales ~  Advertising, data = carseats)

   summary(model_carseats_1)

   model_carseats_1 %>% get_regression_table()


**Confirm the value of the t-statistic using the equation with values for $\hat{\beta_1}$, standard
error, and the information from the null hypothesis (never mind the small rounding error).** $t-
stat = \frac{\hat{\beta_1} - 0}{SE} = \frac{0.114 - 0}{0.02}$

**State your conclusion on whether the coefficient for Advertising is significant or not. State your
decision from the perspective of all 3 approaches i.e.: CI, t-stat, p-value (that you can see in the
table generated by get_regression_table().**

     • CI limits: Limits found are [0.074, 0.155]. The hypothesis is $\hat{\beta_1} = 0$, there‐
      fore since 0 is not inside the CI, we reject the null hypothesis, i.e. coefficient $\beta_1$ is
       significant.

     • t-stat: The t-stat was found to be 5.583, since |5.583|>2, we reject the null hypothesis.

     • p-value: The p-value was found to be 4.38e-08 (i.e. 0) and therefore < 0.05, hence we
      reject the null hypothesis.

All 3 approaches agree on the result of the null hypothesis.

    SOURCE PAGE 3 / 3

     (iii) [5 points] Explain what the t.----() R function is used for. What key pieces of information

    t.----() is used to ---- hypothesis.

     It provides information on:

   Confidence Interval

    t-stat

   p-value t.----(numeric ~ binary) i.e. numeric variable goes first.

   code 1: tb1 <- data %>% group_by(x) %>% mutate(new_y = y – mean(y)) code 2: tb2 <- data
  %>% group_by(x) %>% arrange(z, .by_group = TRUE)

   In code 1 the code results in a data that has been grouped by the x variable and then the
   column y has been centered by group (i.e. every value of y had the average value of its re‐
   spective group taken away from it). In code 2 the code results in a data that has been grouped
   by the x variable and then column z has been arranged in ascending order for each group,
   therefore the final tibble

   tb2 has visibly grouped data by column x, with rows reshuffled such that values of z increase
   within each group of x. Key difference is the dplyr verb mutate vs arrange. Visually mutate will
   not order the rows.

CA09: Group Project 1

----- Group XX

New York City is full of urban wildlife, and rats are one of the city’s most infamous animals. Rats
in NYC are plentiful and in September 2015 a viral video of a brown rat carrying a slice of pizza
down the steps of a NYC subway station in Manhattan created the legend of Pizza Rat .

The source for the data of rat sightings in the city is from NYC’s 311 Service Requests from 2010
to Present . This is a dataset that is pretty much constantly updated and I downloaded this data‐
set on 4-Oct-2025. For this group project, you will use R , dplyr , and ggplot2 to explore and ex‐
plain the data, and tell an interesting story. The data fields are shown below and a full data
dictionary can be found here

1 Loading the data

I have provided some starter code below. A couple comments about it:

     By default, vroom() treats cells that are empty or “NA” as missing values. This rat dataset
     uses “N/A” to mark missing values, so we need to add that as a possible marker of
     missingness (hence na = c("", "NA", "N/A") )

      To make life easier, I always use janitor::clean_names() to remove spaces, upper case
       letters, etc. from variable names.

       I’ve also created a few date-related variables ( sighting_year , sighting_month , sight‐
     ing_day , and sighting_weekday ). You don’t have to use them, but they’re there if you need
     them. The functions that create these, like year() and wday() are part of the lubridate lib‐
       rary.

     There are a few rows with an unspecified borough, so I filtered them out.

          I use str_to_title() to turn the upper case borough into a more legible format, from
    MANHATTAN to Manhattan and from STATEN ISLAND to Staten Island


   # If you get an error "All formats failed to parse. No formats found",

   # rare instances, it might load without the seconds as "09/14/2018 05:00 PM".

2 Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

2.1 Task Description

In the R4DS Exploratory Data Analysis chapter , the authors state:

  “EDA is not a formal process with a strict set of rules. More than anything, EDA is a state of
  mind. During the initial phases of EDA you should feel free to investigate every idea that oc‐
   curs to you. Some of these ideas will pan out, and some will be dead ends. As your exploration
   continues, you will home in on a few particularly productive insights that you’ll eventually write
  up and communicate to others.”

In this section, our goal is to conduct a thorough EDA. The raw data has more than 270,000 rows,
which means you’ll need to aggregate the data ( filter() , group_by() , and summarise() are your
friends).

Recall that an EDA involves three things:

     Looking at the raw values. dplyr::glimpse()

      dplyr::glimpse()

     Computing summary statistics of the variables of interest. skimr::skim() Functions from
      dplyr , such as count() , arrange() , select() , filter() , group_by() , summarise() , and
     mutate() . corrr::correlate() mosaic::favstats()

      skimr::skim()

      Functions from dplyr , such as count() , arrange() , select() , filter() , group_by() ,
     summarise() , and mutate() .

       corrr::correlate()

      mosaic::favstats()

      Creating informative visualizations. ggplot2::ggplot() geom_histogram() or geom_density()
       for numeric continuous variables geom_bar() or geom_col() for categorical variables
      GGally::ggpairs() for scatter plot / correlation matrix Note that you can add transparency to
      points/density plots in the aes call, for example: aes(colour = borough, alpha = 0.4)

      ggplot2::ggplot() geom_histogram() or geom_density() for numeric continuous variables
     geom_bar() or geom_col() for categorical variables

     geom_histogram() or geom_density() for numeric continuous variables

     geom_bar() or geom_col() for categorical variables

      GGally::ggpairs() for scatter plot / correlation matrix Note that you can add transparency to
      points/density plots in the aes call, for example: aes(colour = borough, alpha = 0.4)

     Note that you can add transparency to points/density plots in the aes call, for example:
      aes(colour = borough, alpha = 0.4)




SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  799

PAGE 800
COURSE ----- READER                                                                 Group Assignment 1


You may wish to have a level 1 header ( # ) for your EDA, then use level 2 sub-headers ( ## ) to
make sure you cover all three EDA elements. At a minimum , make sure to include some answer
to these questions in your report:

    How many variables/columns? How many rows/observations?

     Which variables are numbers?

     Which are categorical or factor variables?

       Is there any pattern in the number of sightings per borough, per year, per dwelling type,
       etc., or a combination of these, like the change in the number sightings across the 5
     boroughs between, say, 2015 and 2024.

       Is there any change in rat sighting patterns after systematic shocks, such as covid-19?

     What are the correlations between variables? Does each scatter plot support a linear rela‐
      tionship between variables? Do any of the correlations appear to be conditional on the
     value of a categorical variable?

However, don’t constrain your EDA to the questions above - I’m sure you are able to draw more
interesting insights using the R codes we have seen in class sessions.

A thousand data scientists may explore the data in a thousand different ways. There is not
specific cookbook to follow in EDA. Let your curiosity lead you!

   In all cases, please think about the message your plot is conveying. Don’t just say “This is my
   X-axis, this is my Y-axis”, but rather what’s the so what of the plot. Tell some sort of story and
   speculate about the differences in the patterns in a paragraph.

2.1.1 Plotting figures

For each table, make sure to include a relevant figure. One tip for starting is to draw out on paper
what you want your x- and y-axis to be first and what your geom is; that is, start by drawing the
plot you want ggplot to give you.

Your figure does not have to depict every last number from the data aggregation result. Use your
judgement. It just needs to complement the table, add context, and allow for some sanity
checking both ways.

Think twice about which figures are easy/hard to make, which data formats make better inputs for
plotting functions vs. for human-friendly tables.

2.1.2 Mapping

Visualisations of feature distributions and their relations are key to understanding a data set, and
they can open up new lines of exploration.

While we do not have time to go into all the wonderful geospatial visualisations one can do with
R, you can use the following code to start with a map of your city, and overlay all rat sighting
coordinates to get an overview of the spatial distribution of reported rat activity.

For this visualisation we use the leaflet package, which includes a variety of tools for interactive
maps, so you can easily zoom in-out, click on a point to get the actual location type and date/
time of sighting.

3 Regression

Besides the variables included in the rats tibble, I have also downloaded weather data for NYC
which can be found at the nyc_weather tibble. It may be the case that rats are more active when
it’s warmer? or when it rains?

3.2 Diagnostics, collinearity, summary tables

As you keep building your models, it makes sense to:

     Check the residuals, using autoplot() . You will always have some deviation from normality,
      especially for very high values of n .

     As you start building models with more explanatory variables, make sure you use
      car::vif(model_x) to calculate the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) for your predictors and de‐
     termine whether you have colinear variables. A general guideline is that a VIF larger than
     10 is large, and your model may suffer from collinearity. Remove the variable in question
     and run your model again without it.

     Create a summary table, using huxtable::huxreg() that display your model estimations side
     by side, see which predictors are significant, compare the adjusted \(R^2\) , and the
      Residual Standard Error.

New York City is full of urban wildlife, and rats are one of the city’s most infamous animals. Rats
in NYC are plentiful and in September 2015 [a viral video of a brown rat carrying a slice of pizza
down the steps of a NYC subway station](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3i0_uyGyvis) in
Manhattan created the legend of [Pizza Rat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pizza_Rat).

The source for the data of rat sightings in the city is from NYC's [311 Service Requests from 2010
to Present](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Social-Services/Rat-Sightings/3q43-55fe). This is a data‐
set that is pretty much constantly updated and I downloaded this dataset on 4-Oct-2025. For this
group project, you will use `R`, `dplyr`, and `ggplot2` to explore and explain the data, and tell an
interesting story. The data fields are shown below and a [full data dictionary can be found here]
(https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Social-Services/Rat-Sightings/3q43-55fe)

Loading the data

I have provided some starter code below. A couple comments about it:

     • By default, `vroom()` treats cells that are empty or "NA" as missing values.

This rat dataset uses "N/A" to mark missing values, so we need to add that as a possible marker
of missingness (hence `na = c("", "NA", "N/A")`)

     • To make life easier, I **always** use `janitor::clean_names()` to remove spaces, upper
     case letters, etc. from variable names.



SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  806

PAGE 807
COURSE ----- READER                                                                 Group Assignment 1


     • I've also created a few date-related variables (`sighting_year`, `sighting_month`, `sight‐
      ing_day`, and `sighting_weekday`). You don't have to use them, but they're there if you
     need them.

The functions that create these, like `year()` and `wday()` are part of the **lubridate** library.

     • There are a few rows with an unspecified borough, so I filtered them out.

     • I use `str_to_title()` to turn the upper case borough into a more legible format, from
     `MANHATTAN` to `Manhattan` and from `STATEN ISLAND` to `Staten Island`


   # If you get an error "All formats failed to parse. No formats found",
   # it's because the mdy_hms function couldn't parse the date. The date
   # variable *should* be in this format: "09/14/2018 05:46:05 PM", but in some
   # rare instances, it might load without the seconds as "09/14/2018 05:00 PM".
   # If there are no seconds, use mdy_hm() instead of mdy_hms().

   rats <- vroom::vroom("Rat_Sightings_20251004.zip", na = c("", "NA", "N/A")) %>%
     janitor::clean_names() %>%
     mutate(
     # convert the string to a date format
     created_date = mdy_hms(created_date),

     # just the date without hour info
     sighting_date = as.Date(created_date),

     # get the year, month, etc
     sighting_year = year(created_date),
     sighting_month = month(created_date),
     sighting_month_name = month(created_date, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE),
     sighting_day = day(created_date),
     sighting_weekday = wday(created_date, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)
     ) %>%
     filter(borough != "Unspecified") %>%
     mutate(borough = str_to_title(borough))


Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

Task Description

In the [R4DS Exploratory Data Analysis chapter](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/EDA.html), the authors
state:

> "EDA is not a formal process with a strict set of rules. More than anything, EDA is a state of
mind. During the initial phases of EDA you should feel free to investigate every idea that occurs
to you. Some of these ideas will pan out, and some will be dead ends. As your exploration contin‐
ues, you will home in on a few particularly productive insights that you’ll eventually write up and
communicate to others."

In this section, our goal is to conduct a thorough EDA. The raw data has more than 270,000 rows,
which means you’ll need to aggregate the data (`filter()`, `group_by()`, and `summarise()` are
your friends).

Recall that an EDA involves three things:

     • Looking at the raw values.

     • `dplyr::glimpse()`



SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  807

PAGE 808
COURSE ----- READER                                                                 Group Assignment 1


     • Computing summary statistics of the variables of interest.

     • `skimr::skim()`

     • Functions from **dplyr**, such as `count()`, `arrange()`, `select()`, `filter()`,
      `group_by()`, `summarise()`, and `mutate()`.

     • `corrr::correlate()`

     • `mosaic::favstats()`

     • Creating informative visualizations.

     • `ggplot2::ggplot()`

     • `geom_histogram()` or `geom_density()` for numeric continuous variables

     • `geom_bar()` or `geom_col()` for categorical variables

     • `GGally::ggpairs()` for scatter plot / correlation matrix

     • Note that you can add transparency to points/density plots in the `aes` call, for example:
      `aes(colour = borough, alpha = 0.4)`

You may wish to have a level 1 header (`#`) for your EDA, then use level 2 sub-headers (`##`) to
make sure you cover all three EDA elements. **At a minimum**, make sure to include some
answer to these questions in your report:

     • How many variables/columns? How many rows/observations?

     • Which variables are numbers?

     • Which are categorical or *factor* variables?

     • Is there any pattern in the number of sightings per borough, per year, per dwelling type,
       etc., or a combination of these, like the change in the number sightings across the 5
     boroughs between, say, 2015 and 2024.

     • Is there any change in rat sighting patterns after systematic shocks, such as covid-19?

     • What are the correlations between variables? Does each scatter plot support a linear rela‐
      tionship between variables? Do any of the correlations appear to be conditional on the
     value of a categorical variable?

However, don't constrain your EDA to the questions above - I'm sure you are able to draw more
interesting insights using the R codes we have seen in class sessions.

A thousand data scientists may explore the data in a thousand different ways. There is not
specific cookbook to follow in EDA. Let your curiosity lead you!

> In all cases, please think about the message your plot is conveying. Don’t just say "This is my
X-axis, this is my Y-axis", but rather what’s the **so what** of the plot. Tell some sort of story and
speculate about the differences in the patterns in a paragraph.

Plotting figures

For each table, make sure to include a relevant figure. One tip for starting is to draw out on paper
what you want your x- and y-axis to be first and what your `geom` is; that is, start by drawing the
plot you want `ggplot` to give you.

Mapping

Visualisations of feature distributions and their relations are key to understanding a data set, and
they can open up new lines of exploration. While we do not have time to go into all the wonderful
geospatial visualisations one can do with R, you can use the following code to start with a map of
your city, and overlay all rat sighting coordinates to get an overview of the spatial distribution of
reported rat activity. For this visualisation we use the `leaflet` package, which includes a variety
of tools for interactive maps, so you can easily zoom in-out, click on a point to get the actual loca‐
tion type and date/time of sighting. If you wanted to, you can learn more about `leafelt` the pack‐
age that draws the interactive map, by following [the relevant Datacamp course on mapping with
leaflet](https://www.datacamp.com/courses/interactive-maps-with-leaflet-in-r)


   # let's get the top 7 location types, which account for > 90% of all cases
   # this code generates a vector with the top 7 location types
   top_location_types <- rats %>%
     count(location_type, sort=TRUE) %>%
     mutate(perc = 100*n/sum(n)) %>%
     slice(1:7) %>%
     dplyr::select(location_type) %>%
     pull()

   # lets us choose how to colour each point. What palette and colours to use?
   # A great site to get the relevant color hex codes for maps is
   # https://colorbrewer2.org/#type=qualitative&scheme=Set1&n=7
   my_colours <- c('#e41a1c','#377eb8','#4daf4a','#984ea3','#ff7f00','#ffff33','#a65628')

   # create a function point_fill, that assigns `my_colours` to different location types
   # you can read more here https://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/colors.html
   point_fill <- colorFactor(palette = my_colours,
     rats$location_type)

   rats %>%
     filter(sighting_year == 2024) %>% # just show 2024 data
     filter(location_type %in% top_location_types) %>%
     leaflet() %>%
     addProviderTiles("OpenStreetMap.Mapnik") %>%
     addCircleMarkers(lng = ~longitude,
     lat = ~latitude,
     radius = 1,
     color = ~point_fill(location_type),
     fillOpacity = 0.6,
     popup = ~created_date,
     label = ~location_type) %>%

     addLegend("bottomright", pal = point_fill,
     values = ~location_type,
     title = "2024 Location Type",
     opacity = 0.5)

    SOURCE PAGE 1 / 4

  An aeroplane manufacturing company needs to determine how many hours per day they
   should utilize the 3 robots they have available. Each robot has different energy requirements,
   operating costs, and capabilities that are presented in the following table (all data is given per
   hour of operation)

   The company needs to install at least 1,000,000 rivets and complete 12,800 feet of welding
   per day. Total energy consumed by the robots each day cannot exceed 500 kWh, and each
   robot can work up to 20 hours per day because of maintenance requirements.

   Jean Farell, the operation manager of the company and a graduate, has tried to use optimiza‐
   tion to find the optimal utilization mix of each one of the three robots. She has developed the
   spreadsheet shown in figure 1.1 and used Solver to find the mix that minimises the total cost
   (1.2 shows the formula used in the spreadsheet). Figure 1.3 shows the Solver specification and
   1.4 the result of sensitivity analysis.

   Figure 1.1 The robot utilisation model showing the optimal solution





    SOURCE PAGE 2 / 4

   Figure 1.2 The robot utilization model showing the formulas

   Figure 1.3 The Solver specification





    SOURCE PAGE 3 / 4

   1.4 The Solver sensitivity analysis

         a) What is the solution that minimises the cost (objective function and optimal values

   of the variable).

   The optimal mix results in a total cost of $219.5. This is achieved by using robot type 1 for
   1.22 hours and robot type 3 for 9.76 hours.

         b) What is the meaning of a binding constraint? Which constraints are binding?

  A binding constraint is a constraint that is exactly satisfied at the optimal solution, directly lim‐
    iting the value of the objective function. In this case rivets and energy are binding constraints.

          c) What is the meaning of the reduced cost of robot type 2?




SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  822

PAGE 823
COURSE ----- READER                                                                   Sample Final ----


   The reduced cost indicates how much the objective function coefficient would need to improve
   before the variable robot type 2 would enter the optimal solution. In other words, if we were to
   introduce robot type in the optimal mix, the cost would increase of additional $159.02,
   bringing it to a total of $378.53.

         d) Why is the reduced cost of robot type 1 and 3 equal to zero?

   The two robots are included in the optimal mix, therefore they will not change the value of the
   objective by including them in the mix.





    SOURCE PAGE 4 / 4

         e) Evaluate the impact of increasing the limit on energy from 500 to 520. Why is the
       shadow price of welding equal to zero? The shadow price of the constraint is -1.95. This
       means that for every extra kW the cost reduces of $1.95. The allowable increase is 55.5,
        so the increase from 500 to 520 is within the allowable range, for which the shadow
         price stays constant. The impact on the cost is a decrease of (520-500)*1.95 = $39. The
         constraint on welding is non-binding.

  A ferry service between Liverpool and Belfast can carry various categories of passengers.
   These together with their respective profit margin per trip and loading time, where
   appropriate, are listed below:

   Foot Passengers

   Car with driver and 3 passengers

   0.25

   Coach with driver and 49 passengers

   Lorry with driver

   The ferry can be loaded subject to the following conditions:

   Total Passengers (plus driver) capacity should not exceed 1500 due to safety regulations.

  Maximum number of coaches plus lorries is 25.

  Maximum number of cars is 150 plus four for every lorry or coach space that is not used.

   Vehicle loading time should be 1 hour maximum.

   Market research indicates that maximum demand for foot passengers is 600.

   The profit margins apply whether or not cars and coaches carry the full complement of pas‐
   sengers, but for safety purposes it must be assumed that they are always full.

   Jean Farell, the marketing manager of the company and a graduate, has tried to use optimisa‐
   tion to find the optimal mix of passengers, cars, couches and lorries that the ferry can carry.
   She has developed the spreadsheet shown in Figure 2.1 and used Solver to find the mix that
   maximises the contribution to profit. Figure 2.3 shows the Solver specification and Figure 2.1
   shows the Solver solution obtained. Figure 2.2 shows the formulas of the same model and
   Figure 2.4 shows the Solver sensitivity analysis.

         a) What is the solution that maximises the profit contribution (objective function and
        optimal values of the variables) and which constraints are binding? [2 points]




SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  826

COURSE ----- READER                                                                                                ---- Practice Questions (Part II)


   The optimal loading mix results in a contribution to profit of £11,245. This is achieved by load‐
   ing 600 passengers, 224.5 cars and 1.9 lorries. Clearly the fractional values for cars and lorries
   do not make sense. (See next question).

   The binding constraints are the Total passenger, the Vehicle loading time and the Foot
   passengers constraints.

         b) Jean understands that the fractional values in the solution do not make sense. Find a
         feasible integer solution by rounding the fractional values. You need to check that the
         solution you found satisfies all constrains. [3 points]

  By rounding the results for cars and lorries you can produce the following solution. 600 pas‐
   sengers, 224 cars and 2 lorries. The rounded solution satisfies all constraints and therefore is
   feasible, but note that in general it may not be optimal.

          c) How would you use Excel Solver to find the best integer solution? [5 points]

  We need to add a constraint specifying that our decision variables are integer and resolve.

  By default the Excel Solver will find a solution which is not guaranteed to be optimal, but will
   be within a tolerance from the optimal solution. This is controlled by a Solver option called “In‐
   teger optimality (%). By setting this option to zero, we can force the Solver to search for the
   true optimal solution, but this may increase the solving time. In that case we will no longer get
   the sensitivity analysis results.





    SOURCE PAGE 5 / 5

   Answer the remaining questions based on the solution with fractional values shown in Figure
   2.1 and using the Solver sensitivity analysis in Figure 2.4.

         d) Interpret the reduced cost for the “Coach” variable. [5 points]

   Adding one coach to the optimal ferry loading plan, at the expense of a number of cars and
    lorries, would reduce profits by £26.5. Another interpretation is that the profit margin of
   coaches would need to improve by £26.5 before it becomes optimal to include coaches in the
   optimal loading plan.

         e) Evaluate the impact of increasing the limit on Foot Passengers from 600 to 700. [5
         points]

   The shadow price of the last constraint is 2.4. This means that for every extra foot passenger
  we allow on the ferry, profits go up by £2.4. The allowable increase is 715, so the increase
   from 600 to 700 is within the allowable range, for which the shadow price stays constant. So
   the impact on the profit contribution is an increase of (700-600)*2.4 = £240.

            f) Discuss the effect of increasing the allowable loading time to:

              i) 65 minutes

     ii) 75 minutes.

   [5 points]





SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  827

PAGE 828
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                                ---- Practice Questions (Part II)


   From the dual price of the 4th constraint we see that for every extra minute of loading time we
   can increase profits by £98.7. This dual price holds for increases of up to 9.17 minutes (sensit‐
    ivity analysis results). So increasing the allowed loading time to 65 minutes would add 5 *
   £98.7 = £493.5 to the profit contribution. The impact of an increase of 15 minutes cannot be
   assessed

   using the solution of the base formulation. You would need to reformulate the problem chan‐
   ging the righthand side of the 4th constraint and resolving the problem. One thing you know is
   that the increase in profit will be at least 9.17 * £98.7.

    SOURCE PAGE 1 / 2

  Business Optimisation Exercises— Solutions

   Exercise 1

   (a) At which time segments there are more drivers than the minimum required numbers?

   12:00-16:00, 16:00-20:00 (b) What would the impact be of having 3 more drivers available?

   The shadow price for the constraint on the total number of drivers is €75 and the allowable in‐
   crease infinity. So an extra 3 drivers with increase profit by 75 * 3 = €225. (c) Suppose that
   two drivers are sick and unavailable for work on a given day. What is the financial impact? The
   allowable decrease on the total number of drivers is 4, which greater than

          2. So the shadow price holds for a reduction of 2. Therefore, the decrease in profits is 2 *
       75 = €150. (d) One of the 15 drivers who is available for the shift from 8pm to 4am, has
       been advised by his doctor not to work at nights. What is the effect on the profit contri‐
         bution? There is no impact since the corresponding constraint (Shift20to04) is not
         binding and the shadow price is

          0. (e) Suppose that Euripides finds that the service is slipping during the period from
      8pm to 8am. One approach would be to raise the minimum number of drivers on duty
       between 8pm and midnight. How would this affect profit? Profits will be reduced by €30,
         since the shadow price of the corresponding constraint is -30. (f) Alternatively, the
       minimum number on duty between midnight and

  4am could be raised from 14 to 15. Which alternative is cheaper? In this case the drop in
   profits is €35, so this is more expensive. (g) Another alternative is to ensure that at least one
   driver starts work at 4am. (Currently no one starts at 4am). How would this affect profit?

   The variable “04:00-08:00 Number of drivers”, which corresponds to the number of drivers
   that start work at 4am has currently a value of 0 (i.e. is not optimal), but (unusually) has a re‐
   duced cost of 0. This means that the penalty for introducing that variable to the optimal solu‐
   tion is zero, i.e. we can ensure that at least one driver starts work at 4am without reducing our
    profit.

   Exercise 2

   (a) What is the optimal loan combination and the resulting revenue?

   The optimal loan combination in €(000)s is Unsecured Loans



SEARCHABLE · SOURCE REFERENCED                                                                  829

PAGE 830
COURSE ----- READER                                                                                                ---- Practice Questions (Part II)


   Furniture Loans

   Automobile Loans

    First Home Mortgages

   (b) What is the average return on the amount lent? What is the marginal return (% return on
   an additional £1,000 of loan)? The return on the €1500,000 is 142,500 (from figure 3.1).
   Therefore the average return is 142.5/1500 = 0.095 or 9.5%. The marginal return can be ob‐
   tained by the shadow price of the constraint on Total Investment. This shadow price (0.099)
    tells us that an extra

   unit of investment (€1,000) would give us an increase in return of 0.099 (€000s) which corres‐
   ponds to a 9.9% marginal return. (c) Would the optimal solution change if the return on
   Second Home Mortgages improves by 0.5%? Explain.

   Currently the Annual return of Second hand Mortgages is 8%. At this rate it is not optimal to
   invest in these financial instruments. The reduced cost of this variable in figure 3.3 (-0.01) tells
   us that in order for this variable to become economic to invest the contribution (i.e. the annual
   return) needs to improve by 1%. An improvement of 0.5% is not enough and would have no
   impact.

   (d) What would be the impact of increasing the limit on unsecured loans from 10% to 20%?
   Currently we are limiting the investment on Unsecured Loans to 150 (€000s) which is 10% of
   the overall investment. The shadow price of this constraint (0.03), shows that for every €1000
   of increase in this limit the overall return of the portfolio increases by 0.03 (€000s) i.e. €30.
   The allowable

   increase is 150 (€000s). So the shadow price holds for the increase of the limit from 10% to
  20% of the overall investment which is €150,000. and the impact is 0.03 * 150 = 4.5 (€000s).
   (e) What would be the impact of reducing the minimum requirement of First Home Mortgages
   from €300,000 to €200,000?

   The First Home Mortgages have an annual return of 7% which is the lowest of all available in‐
   vestments. Nevertheless, for policy reasons we are forcing the allocation of at least €300,000
   to this kind of investment. The shadow price of this constraint (-0.02) shows that if we in‐
   crease the limit by €1,000 the overall return drops by 0.02 (€000). Accordingly for every
   €1,000 we decrease

   the limit profits go up by 0.02 (€000). The allowable decrease is 300 (€000s), so the reduction
   of €100,000 we are considering (from €300,000 to €200,000) is within the range that the
  shadow prices hold. The impact of such a change would be an increase in profits of 100 * 0.02
  = 20 (€000s).

   Exercise 1 Vienna Taxi Services (VTS) is a local cab company with operations centred around
   the area of Vienna. They employ 70 drives who work on 8 hour shifts. Demand for cabs in the
   area varies dramatically according to the time of day. The slowest period is between midnight
   and 4am when very few people are going to the airport or taking other long distance trips.
   Euripides, an author and VTS’s manager is has estimated that on average a driver will pick up
  €45 in fares during that period. The average fares per driver for each of the subsequent 4 hour
   period are shown in Table 1.

   Table 1: Fares, Pay & Minimum Numbers of drivers for VTS Time Segment Average Fares Pay
  Minimum number 00:00-04:00 € 45 € 40

   04:00-08:00 € 50 € 40

   08:00-12:00 € 55 € 25

   12:00-16:00 € 60 € 25

   16:00-20:00 € 65 € 25

   20:00-24:00 € 45 € 40

   Even though demand is low in some periods Euripides feels that he must have drivers on duty
   at all times to retain customers and acquire new ones. In order to do this Euripides has de‐
   termined the minimum number of drivers he needs working during each 4 hour time segment
   and these are also shown in table 1 together with the pay that applies in each segment. Thus
   each driver who works

   from 8am to 4pm will be paid €50 and earns fares of €115 on average. However a complica‐
   tion is that only 15 of her drivers will work from 8pm to 4am. Figure 1.1 provides a spread‐
   sheet model that Euripides has built to optimise the allocation of drivers to shifts (showing the
   optimal solution). The decision variables are the cells B14 to B19 containing the number of
   drivers starting

   their shift in each time segment. Using these cells the range B26 to B31 calculate the number
   of drivers working in each shift. There three types of constraints. The first relates to the total
  number of available drivers, the second to the constraint on the number of drivers starting
   their shift at 8pm (15) and the last one relates to the minimum number of drivers in each time

   The amount of unsecured and furniture loans together cannot exceed 20 % of the total.

   The firm can lend a maximum of €1.5 million, of which at least €300,000 should be invested in
    first home mortgages and no more than €375,000 in second home mortgages. The company

Question 2 (25 points)

A ferry service between Liverpool and Belfast can carry various categories of passengers. These
together with their respective profit margin per trip and loading time, where appropriate, are
listed below:

The ferry can be loaded subject to the following conditions:

Total Passengers (plus driver) capacity should not exceed 1500 due to safety regulations.

Maximum number of coaches plus lorries is 25.

Maximum number of cars is 150 plus four for every lorry or coach space that is not used.

Vehicle loading time should be 1 hour maximum.

Market research indicates that maximum demand for foot passengers is 600.

The profit margins apply whether or not cars and coaches carry the full complement of passen‐
gers, but for safety purposes it must be assumed that they are always full.

Jean Farell, the marketing manager of the company and a graduate, has tried to use optimisation
to find the optimal mix of passengers, cars, couches and lorries that the ferry can carry. She has
developed the spreadsheet shown in Figure 2.1 and used Solver to find the mix that maximises
the contribution to profit. Figure 2.3 shows the Solver specification and Figure 2.1 shows the Solv‐
er solution obtained. Figure 2.2 shows the formulas of the same model and Figure 2.4 shows the
Solver sensitivity analysis.

Figure 2.1: The ferry service model showing the optimal solution.

Figure 2.2: The ferry service model showing the formulas

Figure2.3: The Solver Specification

      optimal values of the variables) and which constraints are binding? [2 points]

      b) Jean understands that the fractional values in the solution do not make sense. Find a
      feasible integer solution by rounding the fractional values. You need to check that the
      solution you found satisfies all constrains. [3 points]

      c) How would you use Excel Solver to find the best integer solution? [5 points]

Answer the remaining questions based on the solution with fractional values shown in Figure 2.1

      d) Interpret the reduced cost for the “Coach” variable. [5 points]
